hippo-repro-Q7:
HSIL is a high-grade result, and the high-grade branch of the algorithm has only one exit: colposcopy, immediately. The screening lecture splits abnormal cytology in two. The low-grade group — LSIL and ASC-US — is repeated in 6 to 12 months, because most low-grade change resolves on its own. The high-grade group — HSIL, ASC-H and squamous cell carcinoma — is referred for colposcopy without an intervening test.

C and D are the low-grade arm applied to a high-grade result. Waiting 12 months (C) is the LSIL rule, and repeating the cytology immediately (D) tests the same cells with the same test and cannot downgrade what has already been reported.

B inverts the order of the algorithm. HPV DNA testing sits upstream of cytology in primary HPV screening: a positive HPV sample goes on to cytology, and a positive cytology goes on to colposcopy. Once you are holding an HSIL you are already past the point HPV testing informs, and her postcoital bleeding at 43 makes delay the wrong direction to move in.
hippo-repro-Q10:
Condyloma lata is the lesion of secondary syphilis — large, flat warts, which the lecture is careful to distinguish from the cauliflower-like condylomata acuminata of HPV. It appears alongside the rest of the secondary picture: systemic symptoms, and the characteristic non-itchy rash on the palms and soles.

The other three are the other stages. The painless chancre (A) is primary. Gummatous disease (C) is tertiary. The CNS complications in D — meningitis, stroke, seizures — are neurosyphilis, which the lecture groups with late disease rather than with the secondary stage.

The stage split is the whole point of the question: syphilis is staged by what it is doing to the skin and nervous system at the time, and the treatment (penicillin G) is the same while the stage governs the dose and duration.
hippo-repro-Q12:
Every option listed is a recognised risk factor, which is why E is the answer. The public health lecture groups them rather than listing them flat, and all three named here fall inside the grouping:

  • Age — sexually active youth under 25, who carry a disproportionate share of chlamydia and gonorrhea (B).
  • Behaviour and exposure — injection drug use (A), which is why the lecture treats STIs and bloodborne infections together as STBBIs: the risk factors are shared.
  • Barrier use — no contraception, or a non-barrier method only (C). A non-barrier method prevents pregnancy and does nothing about transmission, and that gap is the point.
  • A previous STI (D), which marks both an exposure pattern and a partner network that has not changed.

A question whose options are all correct is testing whether you will talk yourself out of one. The useful move is to check each against the list rather than hunt for the odd one out.
hippo-repro-Q15:
She meets the Amsel criteria, and the Amsel criteria are how bacterial vaginosis is diagnosed. Any three of four make the diagnosis, and she has three: pH above 4.5 (hers is 5.7), more than 20% clue cells (22%), and a positive amine or “whiff” test. The fourth, a homogeneous grey-white discharge thinly coating the walls, is what she describes.

The whiff test is what excludes the other two infections. The lecture records it as negative in both trichomoniasis and candidiasis, so a positive whiff points away from A and D before you reach anything else.

And the discharge does not fit them either. Trichomonas (A) is profuse, purulent and yellow-green, classically with a strawberry cervix. Candidiasis (D) is thick, white and cottage-cheese-like, adherent to the walls, and itches. Atrophic vaginitis (C) needs a hypoestrogenic state, which a 26-year-old does not have.

The Mirena is not incidental. An intrauterine device is on the lecture's risk-factor list for BV, alongside a new partner, douching and smoking.

hippo-repro-Q16.html:
Read the options against the lecture's own comparison table and B is the one that fails, not C.

C states that candidiasis shows budding yeast, hyphae or pseudohyphae on wet mount while BV shows clue cells. That is exactly what the lecture says, so it is a difference between them.

B has the two treatments the wrong way round. Metronidazole treats bacterial vaginosis; miconazole and fluconazole are the antifungals and treat candidiasis. As written, B is a false statement rather than a real difference, which makes it the option that does not describe how the two conditions differ.

A and D are both genuine differences and are stated correctly: the causative agents (fungal versus a shift to anaerobe-predominant flora — Gardnerella, Mobiluncus, Mycoplasma), and the discharge (thick cottage cheese versus thin grey-white).

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The HippoNotes key gives C. Against 05 - Vaginal Discharge, C is a correct statement of a real difference, and B is the option that reverses the treatments. Treat B as the defensible answer and the printed key as an error. Worth checking with the course before an exam if it matters to you.

hippo-repro-Q23:
Intracardiac digoxin or KCl is a second-trimester step, not a first-trimester one. The lecture's table sets the feticidal injection before misoprostol induction in the second trimester, to 25 weeks. In the first trimester there is nothing for it to do.

The other four are all first-trimester methods:

  • Mifepristone + misoprostol (B), the medical route, to 70 days.
  • Methotrexate + misoprostol (C), the medical route used before mifepristone was approved in Canada in 2015 — less effective and slower, but offered, and to 49 days.
  • Manual vacuum aspiration (A), in the office, to 10 weeks.
  • Dilation and curettage (D), under 14 weeks.

The organising idea is that gestational age picks the method, and the feticidal agent only enters once the gestation is advanced enough to need one.

hippo-repro-Q24.html:
A, B, C and D are all on the lecture's complication list for the procedure itself: uterine perforation, hemorrhage (which may signal uterine atony, low implantation or a larger gestational age than expected), hematometra or post-abortal syndrome, and cervical shock. Infertility is not among them, which is what the key is pointing at.

Read it as “not an immediate complication” rather than “never a consequence”. The same lecture names curettage as a risk factor for intrauterine adhesions — about 8% after one procedure, rising towards 30% by a third within 24 hours — and trauma as the major cause of them. Adhesions are the mechanism behind Asherman syndrome, which does impair fertility.

So the distinction the question is really drawing is between what can go wrong during and just after a D&C and what can follow from repeated instrumentation over time.

flags.title: True only of the immediate complications
flags.html: The key treats infertility as not a complication of D&C. That holds for the immediate complications, but 01 - Abortion in Canada lists curettage as the leading cause of intrauterine adhesions, and adhesions (Asherman syndrome) can impair fertility. The answer is defensible; the option is not as clean as it looks.

module-repro-Q6:
Estrogen proliferates the endometrium; the progestin is there to oppose it. The pharmacology lecture lists endometrial proliferation among estrogen's actions, and lists reduced endometrial carcinoma among the benefits of a combined preparation. Unopposed estrogen drives the endometrium; adding a progestin is what keeps that from becoming hyperplasia and then carcinoma. The same combined preparation also lowers the risk of ovarian cyst, ovarian cancer and pelvic inflammatory disease.

A is the risk that moves the other way. The lecture states plainly that giving exogenous estrogen and progesterone can raise the risk of breast cancer, and breast cancer is a contraindication to combined hormonal contraception rather than an indication for it.

B and D are not what the progestin is doing. Cervical cancer is driven by persistent high-risk HPV, and neither cancer is on the lecture's list of what a combined preparation protects against.

hippo-repro-Q31.html:
Leiomyomas are the most common neoplasm in females — clinically apparent in about 25% of reproductive-age women — and the most common cause of abnormal uterine bleeding. They are benign smooth-muscle tumours, and the lecture is emphatic that they are not pre-malignant and not a precursor to malignancy.

The distractors are each a different kind of thing, which is what the question is really testing. An endometrial polyp (A) is a focal overgrowth and is common, but not on leiomyoma's scale. Adenomyosis (B) is endometrial glands within the myometrium — a process, not a neoplasm. Endometrial hyperplasia (D) is proliferation that is on the pathway to carcinoma, which makes it the conceptual opposite of a fibroid rather than a competitor for the same title.

review.t: Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain

hippo-repro-Q34:
Each germ cell tumour is named by the tissue it is trying to be, and the marker follows from that. The lecture's marker table sets out three strong associations:

  • Dysgerminoma → LDH. The ovarian counterpart of the seminoma; LDH is its marker.
  • Yolk sac tumour → alpha-fetoprotein. AFP is what a yolk sac makes, so a tumour differentiating towards yolk sac makes it too. Most common in toddlers, and Schiller-Duval bodies on histology are pathognomonic.
  • Choriocarcinoma → beta-hCG. It arises from placental tissue, and beta-hCG is the placental hormone.

Worth holding onto: immature teratoma and embryonal carcinoma each raise two of the three weakly, which is why the table marks the three above as the strong, discriminating associations rather than the only ones.
hippo-repro-Q36:
All four are on the examination list, so E is right. The lecture groups them by what they are actually showing you, which is more useful than the list itself:

  • Acanthosis nigricans (A), over the back of the neck and in the axilla, usually with skin tags beside it. These are the insulin resistance signs.
  • Hirsutism (B) — terminal hair in a male pattern: face, chin, chest, upper arms.
  • Acne (C) and frontal alopecia (D), which sit with hirsutism as the androgen signs.

One caution the lecture attaches to the same list: rate of onset, ethnicity and parental appearance all have to be weighed before hair growth is called abnormal, and a rapid onset is the androgen-secreting tumour question rather than the PCOS one.

Note this material is taught in the endocrinology block, under the name PMOS, not in reproduction.
hippo-repro-Q40:
The lecture's definition is exact: post-menopausal bleeding is any bleeding in a post-menopausal woman after the absence of menstrual flow for 12 months. It occurs in about 11% of post-menopausal women.

The threshold is doing real work rather than being a number to memorise. Twelve months is also what defines menopause itself, so the definition is saying that bleeding counts as post-menopausal once you are confident menopause has actually happened. Shorter intervals (A, C) fall inside perimenopause, where an irregular cycle is expected rather than alarming, and two years (B) would delay investigation of a symptom whose whole point is that it needs endometrial carcinoma excluded.
hippo-repro-Q43:
A and D both follow from the same event: the ovary stops responding. The remaining few oocytes become unresponsive to gonadotropins, so estrogen and progesterone production falls.

That falling estrogen is what causes A. Vasomotor symptoms — hot flashes, night sweats, perspiration, chills, palpitations — are the most prevalent symptoms, in 80–85% during menopause. Vaginal burning and dryness belong to the genitourinary group, alongside dyspareunia, dysuria, urgency and recurrent urinary tract infections.

And it is what causes D. With the ovary no longer producing estrogen, the negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost, so LH and FSH rise. A raised FSH is the biochemical signature of menopause for exactly this reason.

B and C invert it. Estrogen and progesterone production falls rather than rises (C), and low estrogen means less vaginal hydration, not more (B) — that dryness is the same finding the question already gave you in A.
hippo-repro-Q44:
A is true because the progestin in HRT has one job: protecting the endometrium. Unopposed estrogen drives endometrial proliferation, so a woman with a uterus needs a progestin alongside it. After hysterectomy there is no endometrium to protect, so estrogen-only therapy is appropriate.

D and E are the perimenopausal transition as the lecture describes it. Cycle length and flow change first (D), and the pattern then moves through oligomenorrhea and hypomenorrhea until menstruation stops altogether (E).

B fails on the therapy, not the symptoms. Palpitations and perspiration are genuinely vasomotor symptoms, but local estrogen therapy is local: it treats the genitourinary symptoms — dryness, dyspareunia, urinary symptoms — and systemic therapy is what addresses vasomotor symptoms.

C misstates the list. The three main causes of illness and disability named for this group are cardiovascular disease, cancer, and osteoporosis-associated fractures. Reduced sexual drive is common — half of women report at least one sexual problem, most often reduced desire — but it is not one of the three, and stroke sits inside cardiovascular disease rather than beside it.
hippo-repro-Q46:
A large uterus is a contraindication to every minimally invasive route, so the abdominal approach is what is left. That is the pattern to take from this rather than the single answer: the lecture lists “large uterus” under contraindications for the vaginal approach (B), for laparoscopic-assisted vaginal hysterectomy (C), and for total or subtotal laparoscopic hysterectomy (D).

The routes are otherwise ranked the other way round. The lecture is explicit that if a patient's anatomy is amenable to a vaginal approach, that should be the first option, and the laparoscopic routes are framed as alternatives to an abdominal hysterectomy rather than as the default. Abdominal is the fallback when anatomy rules the others out, which is precisely the situation an enlarged uterus creates.

The vaginal route carries other contraindications worth holding alongside it: prior pelvic surgery, extensive scarring, a narrow introitus or pelvis, poor uterine descent, and a planned salpingectomy or salpingo-oophorectomy, since the tubes and ovaries are not readily reached through the vagina.

workbook-repro-Q89.html:
The figure comes straight from the lecture: congenital anomalies occur in 2–3% of all pregnancies, with the degree of severity varying widely across that group.

It is worth pairing with the scan itself. Every pregnant person in Canada is offered a fetal anatomy scan between 18 and 22 weeks, and screening for major anatomical congenital anomalies is its main purpose. A 2–3% background rate is what makes a universal scan worth doing and also what keeps its yield modest, which is the tension the question is really about.

workbook-repro-Q113:
Labour is divided by what the cervix and the fetus are doing, and the second stage is the pushing stage: full dilation through to delivery of the fetus.

The other options are the neighbouring stages, which is what makes them worth knowing rather than eliminating:

  • A is the first stage: onset of labour to full dilation. It subdivides into a latent phase (0–4 cm) and an active phase (4–10 cm).
  • B describes a point inside the active phase, not a stage. True labour is defined by regular uterine contractions causing progressive cervical dilation, so a single dilation figure never defines a stage.
  • D is the third stage, ending with expulsion of the placenta.
  • E is the autotransfusion of the third and fourth stages, when up to 500 mL returns from the uteroplacental unit to the maternal circulation.
workbook-repro-Q121:
The Kleihauer-Betke test detects fetal red cells that have crossed into maternal blood, and for that to happen there must be a breach of the fetomaternal interface — the placenta shearing away from the uterine wall.

That mechanism is what separates abruption from the other causes of antepartum bleeding here. In placenta previa (A) the placenta is implanted over the os and bleeds from the maternal side without necessarily being torn off it. In vasa previa (B) the bleeding is fetal in origin but comes from unprotected fetal vessels crossing the membranes, so it leaves the fetus rather than entering the maternal circulation. Gestational trophoblastic disease (D) and ectopic pregnancy (E) are not placental separation at all.
hippo-repro-Q1:
From 16 - Approach to Sexual Health. The refractory period is the lecture's single starred sex difference in the Masters & Johnson cycle: at resolution the male is physiologically incapable of another orgasm or ejaculation for a time, while the female has no refractory period and can have multiple orgasms. D states exactly the reverse, so it is the mismatched pair.

  • A is correctly matched: excitement brings penile erection, and in females breast enlargement and nipple erection (NO-driven engorgement).
  • B is correctly matched: plateau is when the coronal ridge increases in circumference and the uterus becomes fully elevated (it only begins to elevate in excitement).
  • C ("organism" = orgasm) is correctly matched: bladder-sphincter spasm then contraction of vas deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate (emission) in males; rhythmic vaginal-wall contractions at 0.8-s intervals in females.
hippo-repro-Q3:
From 06 - Pathology of the Breast. Sort by the tissue of origin. Fat necrosis arises in the interlobular stroma/fat, often after trauma, and presents as a firm, irregular mass ± erythema, skin retraction and dimpling - the benign lesion that mimics cancer. Bloody nipple discharge belongs to a large-duct lesion, the intraductal papilloma (30s-50s, tan-pink friable lesion in a dilated duct), so A is the mismatch.

  • B is correct: fibroadenoma is a discrete, mobile, rubbery mass of women in their 20s-30s.
  • C is correct: acute mastitis is the lecture's tense, hot, painful breast, usually lactational Staph/Strep.
  • D is correct: fibrocystic change is lumpy breast tissue that fluctuates with the menstrual cycle - physiological, not pathological.
hippo-repro-Q4:
From 06 - Pathology of the Breast and 07 - Approach to Common Breast Problems. The reproductive-history risk factors for breast cancer all come down to more lifetime cycles of unopposed estrogen/progesterone on breast epithelium: early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, older age at first pregnancy, and no breastfeeding. Each pregnancy (and lactation) interrupts cycling and matures the lobules, so multiparity is protective - the opposite of a risk factor.

  • A early menarche lengthens cycling exposure - listed minor factor (RR 1.1-1.3).
  • B alcohol is listed (> 2 drinks/day).
  • D not breastfeeding is listed alongside nulliparity.
hippo-repro-Q9:
From 08 - Approach to Sexually Transmitted Infections. Split the list by what can be sampled directly. Syphilis will not grow in culture, so it is diagnosed by darkfield microscopy and serology (VDRL screen, fluorescent treponemal antibody to confirm). Hepatitis B is read off a serology panel (HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, anti-HBs). HIV is diagnosed by the HIV 1/2 Ag/Ab combination immunoassay. That is iii, iv, v.

  • A, B, C each include chlamydia and/or gonorrhea, which are diagnosed by direct sampling of the organism - cervical/vaginal swab or first-catch urine > 2 h since voiding (NAAT) - not by antibodies.

Principle: bloodborne/systemic infections are serology; mucosal bacterial STIs are swab or urine.
hippo-repro-Q11:
From 07 - Public Health and STIs. The lecture's local epidemiology is explicit: chlamydia is the commonest STI in London, and the STI lecture adds that it is the most common STI overall with very high rates in London, Ontario - largely because it is so often asymptomatic and goes untreated in young people.

  • C gonorrhea is the distractor that is rising locally (with syphilis), but it has not overtaken chlamydia.
  • D HIV rates have been stable, and at far lower numbers.
  • B hepatitis C is a bloodborne infection driven mainly by injection drug use, not the leading sexually transmitted infection.

hippo-repro-Q13.html:
BRATS lists the observable genital injuries documented on examination: Bruises, Redness, Abrasions, Tears, Swelling. Each is a physical sign the examiner can see and record as medico-legal evidence.

  • A-D (bruises, redness, abrasions, tears) are all genuine letters of the mnemonic.
  • E fails because soreness is a symptom the survivor reports, not a sign the examiner documents - which is why the S is swelling.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note in the vault covers the acute sexual assault exam or the BRATS mnemonic; the only mention of assault is as an STI risk circumstance in 07 - Public Health and STIs. The reasoning here is from general principles, not from the week's material.

hippo-repro-Q27:
From 12 - Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain. Primary dysmenorrhea has no abnormal laboratory or physical findings (B), which is why the lecture stars it as purely a clinical diagnosis from history (A). Treatment follows the mechanism: NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, and ovulatory suppression (OCP, hormonal IUD) thins the endometrium so less is sloughed (C).

  • D fails on one word. The cascade is prostaglandins from endometrial sloughing → contractions → uterine pressure exceeds arterial pressure → ischaemia → anaerobic metabolites → stimulation of type C pain neurons (the slow, unmyelinated fibres of dull cramping visceral pain), not type A.
hippo-repro-Q29:
From 12 - Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain and 11 - Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain. Chronic pelvic pain is defined by time: pain below the umbilicus for at least 6 months, severe enough to cause disability or need treatment. A ruptured ovarian cyst is a single event - sudden pain, sometimes a falling Hb, classically 2-3 weeks from the LMP - and sits in the acute pelvic pain lecture beside ectopic, PID and torsion.

  • A-D are the columns of the chronic pelvic pain chart itself: primary dysmenorrhea (with menses, days 1-2), endometriosis (pain ~2 days before menses), adenomyosis (boggy uterus + menorrhagia), and fibroids (pressure, AUB) - all recurrent, cyclical or persistent.

hippo-repro-Q30.html:
From 13 - Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain. The lecture's differential table of benign uterine lesions has a "Hormone responsive" row, and it reads yes for all of them:

  • A Endometrial polyp - growth is hormone dependent, linked to estrogen and tamoxifen.
  • C Leiomyoma - grows rapidly in pregnancy and regresses at menopause or after oophorectomy.
  • B Adenomyosis - also marked yes, and the chronic pelvic pain lecture treats it with hormonal suppression, danazol and GnRH agonists, which only works on a hormone-responsive lesion.

The column where adenomyosis is the lone "no" is infertility (and neoplasm, which it shares with polyps). The key most likely reflects that column rather than hormone dependence.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: 13 - Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain lists adenomyosis as hormone responsive (yes), the same as polyps and leiomyomas, so none of the three options is "not hormone-dependent" on the lecture's own table. The HippoNotes key (B) is kept as printed; treat this question as unreliable unless the source slide says otherwise.

hippo-repro-Q32: From 04 - Approach to and Pathology of a Pelvic Mass. A borderline epithelial tumour has complex architecture and atypical cells but no frank stromal invasion; it is pre-cancerous, excised, and usually has a very good prognosis. The lecture lists what it can do - form implants (serous subtype only), adhere, recur, and progress to a low-grade carcinoma. High-grade serous carcinoma arises by a different route (the fallopian-tube STIC / p53 pathway), not from a borderline precursor - so "True" (A) fails.

hippo-repro-Q33.html: From 04 - Approach to and Pathology of a Pelvic Mass. The lecture's four bullets on malignant epithelial tumours map almost one-to-one onto the options: serous carcinoma is the #1 form of "ovarian cancer" (A, true), often advanced stage at presentation - hence the high mortality (C, true), post-menopausal, younger if familial (D, true), and bilaterality common, except mucinous (B, false - it says unilateral). B is therefore the one statement that does not fit, which is what the key and its rationale identify.

flags.title: The stem and the key disagree
flags.html: The stem says "select all that applies", which on 04 - Approach to and Pathology of a Pelvic Mass would be A, C, D. The key (B) and its rationale only make sense if the stem meant "which is NOT true". The key is kept as printed; read the stem as an EXCEPT question.

hippo-repro-Q38:
From 10 - Endometriosis, 13 - Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain and endometrioma. (The stem's image is not in this note, so the reasoning rests on the key's own description of the lesion.)

A cyst leaking thick, dark old blood is an endometrioma - the chocolate cyst of the ovary, the adnexal-mass form of endometriosis (present in 17-44% of patients). Cyclic bleeding of ectopic endometrium into a closed ovarian cyst concentrates old blood and hemosiderin.

  • A and B fail on the pairing: "blueberry" (early) and "powder burn" (late) lesions are the lecture's peritoneal endometriosis lesions, not leiomyoma, which is a round, well-circumscribed, whorled smooth-muscle nodule.
  • D names the right disease, but a peritoneal window is a peritoneal defect, not a fluid-filled cyst leaking old blood.
hippo-repro-Q39:
From 10 - Endometriosis. Tubal occlusion appears in the lecture under complications, not treatment: endometriosis causes infertility partly via tubal occlusion (and impaired tubal transport from an inflamed pelvis). Occluding the tubes does nothing to estrogen-driven ectopic endometrium or its pain.

  • A NSAIDs - the mainstay is ovulatory suppression plus NSAID pain control.
  • B danazol - a testosterone derivative giving pseudomenopause (withdraws estrogen), alongside GnRH agonists.
  • C NuvaRing (vaginal contraceptive ring) - a pseudopregnancy option with the OCP, patch, Depo and hormonal IUS.
  • D hysterectomy ± oophorectomy - the definitive treatment; not first line and not for those wanting fertility, but still a treatment.
hippo-repro-Q53:
From 02 - Dilation and Curettage. The lecture lists all six complications by the step that causes them but does not rank them by frequency; the frequency ordering below is from general principles.

The three common ones are the everyday failures of evacuating a pregnant uterus: infection from instrumentation (hence prophylaxis for therapeutic abortion), hemorrhage from atony, low implantation or larger gestational age, and retained products of conception from incomplete evacuation (secondary D&C or misoprostol).

  • B uterine perforation (during dilatation or suction) is serious but uncommon - the rarity is why it prompts finishing under ultrasound or laparoscopic guidance.
  • D hematometra (post-abortal syndrome) is an uncommon post-procedure event requiring immediate re-evacuation.
  • E Asherman syndrome is a late sequel of curettage - above all repeat or sharp curettage - not an immediate common complication.
hippo-repro-Q60:
From 16 - Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada. The lecture's CVS-vs-amnio table gives amniocentesis (15-20 wk) a miscarriage risk of 1/800, ~0.5%, and no other listed risk - it samples fetal cells shed into amniotic fluid, so it is also the more accurate test.

  • B ~1% (1/400) is the CVS miscarriage figure - the price of sampling earlier.
  • C maternal cell contamination and D confined placental mosaicism are both CVS problems because CVS samples placenta, not fetus: maternal decidua can contaminate it, and a placenta-only chromosomal change gives a false positive.
hippo-repro-Q80:
From neonatal sepsis (the reference note embedded in 09 - Approach to Neonatal Care). FHR accelerations are the reassuring feature of a normal tracing - a well-oxygenated fetus with an intact autonomic response - so they mark lower, not higher, risk. The risk-factor list names fetal decelerations instead, as a sign of fetal compromise.

  • A preterm labour/preterm delivery (≤ 36 wk) - listed; preterm birth carries sepsis at 1/250 vs 1/1000 at term.
  • B meconium in the amniotic fluid - listed (↑ risk 2x); meconium passage is itself a sign of fetal distress.
  • D chorioamnionitis - listed (↑ risk 4x).
  • E untreated maternal GBS - Group B strep is the starred common organism, reduced by routine GBS testing and intrapartum prophylaxis.
hippo-repro-Q83:
From 05 - Abnormal Labour. Induction is indicated for any condition that raises maternal or fetal morbidity, and the lecture's list names "maternal disease (e.g., cardiac); significant maternal cardiac, respiratory, renal, or hematologic conditions". A planned, monitored induction lets the team control timing and staffing rather than waiting for spontaneous labour - so "delay induction" is the false statement.

  • A true: post dates heads the indication list (and ARRIVE supports low-risk IOL at 39 wk).
  • B true: step ① is cervical ripening, chemical (prostaglandins - dinoprostone, misoprostol) or mechanical (Foley).
  • C true: artificial rupture of membranes may start labour on its own once the cervix is ~2 cm.
  • E true: IV synthetic oxytocin starts contractions, with continuous fetal monitoring.
hippo-repro-Q84:
From 05 - Abnormal Labour. Operative vaginal delivery exists to expedite the 2nd stage, and the 2nd stage only begins at full dilation. The gate is full dilation + engaged vertex + ruptured membranes + no CPD; pulling a head through an incompletely dilated cervix tears the cervix and fails, so incomplete dilation is an absolute contraindication (with unengaged head, non-vertex/face/brow, CPD, fetal coagulopathy/demineralization).

  • A true: malpresentation as OT or OP is a listed fetal indication, and rotation is why forceps (traction + rotation) rather than vacuum (traction only; relative contraindication > 45°) is chosen.
  • C true: atypical/abnormal FHR tracing is starred as the #1 reason.
  • D true: the two instruments are forceps and vacuum.
hippo-endo-Q1:
From 01 - Intro to Diabetes. T1DM is autoimmune beta-cell destruction, and the lecture's autoantibody panel is insulin/proinsulin, GAD, IA-2 and ZnT8 ("Zn18" in the key is a typo for ZnT8). GAD is the most specific marker (positive in ~70%). Remember too that the number of antibodies carries the risk, not their presence: one alone does not raise risk above baseline, three means ~40% in 5 years.

  • A, B alone are each true but incomplete, since both belong to the panel.
  • C (anti-M) is not part of the T1DM panel. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies point to primary biliary cholangitis, not the beta cell.
  • E fails because C is wrong.
hippo-endo-Q8:
From 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes and 10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes. New vessels are the defining feature of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, the stage that is vision-threatening and must be treated. The new vessels are fragile and bleed into the vitreous. The notes' management is urgent ophthalmology for laser ± vitrectomy, alongside tighter glycemic control (DCCT: intensive control ↓ progression of existing retinopathy).

  • A mislabels the stage: pre-proliferative disease means cotton wool spots, exudates and macular edema, with no new vessels, and it is managed by monitoring.
  • B leaves a sight-threatening lesion untreated.
  • C is wrong because neovascularization is ischemic retinal disease, not a hematologic problem.
hippo-endo-Q9:
From 10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes. In DCCT (T1DM, 6.5 years), intensive therapy (≥3 injections/day or a pump, A1c target <7%) cut new retinopathy by 76% (primary prevention) and worsening of existing retinopathy by 54% (secondary prevention). That makes B true. It also cut clinical neuropathy by 60% and microalbuminuria by 39%, which makes C true. The cost was 2-3× more hypoglycemia, and there was no macrovascular benefit within the trial.

  • A fails on "only": the benefit covered all the microvascular endpoints.
  • E fails because it discards B, which the secondary-prevention arm confirms.
hippo-endo-Q11:
From 08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes. The lecture's point is that HbA1c is the target and SMBG is how you get there. The notes list what SMBG does:

  • it gives real-time feedback on whether the patient is at target (A)
  • it is needed to prevent hypoglycemia in anyone on insulin or a secretagogue, and to confirm and treat an episode (B)
  • it guides medication decisions, including pre-meal bolus doses (C)

SMBG is also the only way to assess control when the A1c is unreliable.

  • D fails because it drops C: clinician dose titration is one of the listed uses.
  • A, B or C alone would each be incomplete, and none is offered on its own anyway.
hippo-endo-Q15:
From 03 - Pharmacology of Insulin. Insulin binds its receptor only as a monomer, so onset and duration depend on one thing: how fast monomers dissociate from the hexamer. Whatever stabilizes the hexamer slows release and lengthens action:

  • zinc/protamine in NPH
  • microprecipitates at neutral pH for glargine
  • self-aggregation plus albumin binding for detemir
  • multi-hexamers for degludec

The mechanism at the receptor is identical for every preparation. They differ only in pharmacokinetics.

  • A confuses zinc (which does stabilize hexamers) with iron, which plays no part.
  • B fails because insulin is injected subcutaneously, so there is no first-pass hepatic metabolism, and first-pass loss would shorten action, not prolong it.
hippo-endo-Q16:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs. Sulfonylureas close the beta-cell K-ATP channel and release insulin glucose-independently, so insulin keeps flowing even when glucose is already low. That is why the notes say not to give them to the elderly, people living alone or people who drive for a living, and why the risk rises in liver or kidney failure.

  • A: metformin is a sensitizer that does not change insulin release, so it carries low hypoglycemia risk as monotherapy.
  • C: SGLT2 inhibitors work at the proximal tubule, independently of insulin and the beta cell, so their risk is low.
  • D: GLP-1RAs are secretagogues, but glucose-dependent ones, so they greatly reduce the risk.
  • E pairs two low-risk agents.
hippo-endo-Q18:
From naltrexone-bupropion and 09 - Introduction to Obesity. The obesity lecture ranks the agents tirzepatide > semaglutide > naltrexone-bupropion > orlistat. The drug note for Contrave lists one serious adverse effect: ↑ risk of suicidal thoughts in patients with depression. Its bupropion component acts centrally on noradrenergic/dopaminergic POMC circuits. A positive PHQ-9 therefore makes it the agent to avoid until the depression is assessed and managed.

  • A Orlistat blocks gut lipase and acts peripherally. Its problems are GI and limited efficacy, not mood.
  • B, C semaglutide and liraglutide are GLP-1 agonists whose limiting effects in the notes are GI upset and pancreatitis, with no psychiatric warning.
hippo-endo-Q19:
From 09 - Introduction to Obesity and sleeve gastrectomy. All three statements match the vault:

  • A: sleeve gastrectomy removes 75-85% of the stomach, leaving a banana-sized tube of roughly 15-25%. It is a purely restrictive procedure.
  • B: because it has no bypass or anastomosis, it is "more often considered for those at high operative risk".
  • C: the lecture states that laparoscopic gastric banding is no longer performed and is explicitly not recommended. Sleeve and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass are the two most common operations.

Since A, B and C are all true, D is the only complete answer.
hippo-endo-Q23:
From 01 - Thyroid and Parathyroid Gland Physiology and 02 - Drugs Affecting Calcium Homeostasis. Vitamin D's effect on bone flips with the serum calcium. When calcium is low, calcitriol drives osteoclastic resorption to release calcium into the blood, alongside ↑ gut absorption. Only when calcium is high does it favor mineralization by osteoblasts. This patient is hypocalcemic, so in the short term vitamin D will pull calcium out of bone.

  • B gets the direction backwards: formation and mineralization is the high-calcium response.
  • C, D fail on "regardless". The whole point is that the effect depends on the calcium level, and the notes flag "resorption regardless" as a classic trap.

hippo-endo-Q32.html:
The key discriminator is whether the factor is already counted inside FRAX/CAROC. Osteoporosis Canada's moderate-risk "consider treatment" factors are the ones the calculators miss:

  • recurrent falls (A)
  • aromatase-inhibitor therapy (C) and androgen-deprivation therapy (E), which both cause rapid hypogonadal bone loss
  • vertebral fracture on imaging, and long-term glucocorticoids
  • B fails because parental fracture history is already an input to FRAX, so it has been counted once and should not push the patient up a second time. The standard FRAX input is also parental hip fracture, not vertebral.
  • D fails for the same reason: current smoking is a FRAX input.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: 06 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Osteoporosis covers the risk bands (moderate = 10-20% 10-year risk) and the steroid and prior-fracture modifiers, but not this list. The reasoning here is from general principles (Osteoporosis Canada / FRAX), not from the week's material.

hippo-endo-Q35:
From 07 - Overview of Metabolic Bone Disease. The lecture says the lab panel separates the three metabolic bone diseases before imaging, and this panel is osteomalacia's signature. Osteomalacia is a mineralization defect from vitamin D deficiency:

  • calcium AND phosphate are both low, with a high ALP
  • it causes proximal myopathy, which osteoporosis never does
  • the x-ray shows pseudofractures (Looser zones)
  • A Paget's has normal calcium and phosphate with a very high ALP, and a cotton-wool, expanded, dense bone picture.
  • B osteoporosis has a normal panel and is indolent until a fragility fracture, with no myopathy.
  • C osteogenesis imperfecta is a collagen defect with a normal panel, blue sclerae and fractures from birth.
hippo-endo-Q38:
From 09 - Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis. GnRH comes from parvicellular hypothalamic neurons, whose axons end in the median eminence. There it enters the primary capillary plexus, travels down the hypophysial portal veins, and reaches the secondary plexus of the anterior pituitary. It acts on GnRH receptors on gonadotropes, which release LH and FSH into the systemic circulation. The portal system keeps GnRH concentrated, which matters because it acts in pulses at very low amounts.

  • A, C name the posterior pituitary. That is where magnocellular axons end, releasing oxytocin and vasopressin directly into the blood. The posterior pituitary makes no gonadotropins.
  • B has the right target but the wrong route: GnRH does not go through the general circulation to reach the pituitary.
hippo-endo-Q39:
From 09 - Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis. The lecture's pulse-generator table groups the regulators:

  • positive: glutamate, NPY, norepinephrine, and kisspeptin, the strongest
  • negative: GABA and endogenous opioids

So A is the false statement. The pre-pubertal GABA brake lifting is what restarts puberty. B, C and D are all true:

  • B is true: pulses are obligatory, because continuous GnRH desensitizes the receptor and shuts the axis down. That is how GnRH agonists produce chemical castration.
  • C is true: estradiol and progesterone do not act on the GnRH neuron itself. They act on other neurons that synapse onto it.
  • D is true: the rhythm is intrinsic, since cultured GnRH neurons still release in coordinated pulses in vitro.
hippo-endo-Q41:
From 10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle. Estradiol is the one hormone that reverses the sign of its own feedback. Below threshold it suppresses FSH. Held above 300-500 pg/mL for about 48 hours, at the end of the follicular phase, it switches the GnRH response to feed-forward and triggers the mid-cycle LH and FSH surge. The surge needs both the level and the duration, which is exactly what "reaches and maintains" in A captures.

  • B inverts the mechanism: the surge follows a sustained rise in estrogen, not a fall that removes negative feedback.
  • C treats GnRH pulse strength as the cause, when it is only the consequence of estradiol's switch.
  • D gets the timing wrong: the corpus luteum forms after ovulation, so its progesterone comes after the surge.
hippo-endo-Q43:
From 10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle and 09 - Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis. This is the two-cell mechanism:

  • LH acts on theca cells, which convert cholesterol to androgen.
  • FSH acts on granulosa cells, which carry the aromatase that turns that androgen into estradiol.

Neither cell can make estradiol alone. The male mirror is LH on Leydig cells and FSH on Sertoli cells.

  • A, D name steroid products as the stimulating hormones. Estrogen and progesterone are what these cells make, not the hormones that drive them.
  • C fails because GnRH acts on anterior-pituitary gonadotropes. It never reaches the gonad.
hippo-endo-Q44:
From 01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease. Christian has shock, profound dehydration and hypoglycemia, which is the picture of adrenal crisis: loss of cortisol's support of vascular tone and gluconeogenesis. The lecture's rule is 2-3 L saline/dextrose plus hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus, without waiting for results. He is the only one who can die within hours. The other three are chronic syndromes to work up electively:

  • A Archibald has weakness, anorexia and salt craving, which is chronic primary adrenal insufficiency. It needs diagnosis and replacement, but he is not in shock.
  • B Bastien has resistant hypertension with low K⁺, the pattern of Conn syndrome, which is worked up with aldosterone/renin.
  • D Damien has proximal wasting, purple striae >1 cm and ecchymoses, which is Cushing syndrome: important, but not an emergency.
hippo-endo-Q49:
From 03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty. The lecture insists that the vocabulary is not interchangeable. Adrenarche is a separate, adrenal axis, with adrenal androgens producing pubic and axillary hair, body odour and acne. It is independent of gonadal function, which is why Turner girls have 100% pubarche with streak ovaries. B wrongly attributes it to the gonads. The other three statements are true:

  • A is true: after menarche the axis stays immature, and irregular anovulatory cycles for >2 years are normal.
  • C is true: gonadarche is defined as the gonads being activated by LH and FSH.
  • D is true: thelarche is breast development driven by ovarian estradiol.
hippo-endo-Q50:
From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. The lecture gives the girls' sequence as thelarche → growth spurt → pubarche → menarche:

  • Thelarche (C) is the first sign in most girls, at about 10.3 years. Ovarian estradiol drives breast development.
  • The growth spurt (A) comes early in girls, at Tanner 2-3 (in boys it comes later, at Tanner 3-4, which is why boys finish taller).
  • Pubarche (D) follows.
  • Menarche (B) comes last, at about 12.7 years, roughly 2.5 years after thelarche.

Two traps:

  • 15% of girls have pubarche first, because it is adrenal rather than gonadal, so the order is typical, not invariant.
  • Menarche is never early in the sequence: it needs enough estradiol and progesterone to build and shed endometrium, which comes after peak height velocity.
hippo-endo-Q51:
From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. Delayed puberty is defined statistically as the absence or incomplete development of puberty at an age 2.5 SD above the population mean. That works out to 13 years for girls and 14 years for boys. So B's 15-year cut-off is not the accepted definition, and waiting until 15 would delay the workup (karyotype, LH/FSH, bone age) by a year. The other three are accepted:

  • A matches the girls' cut-off of 13.
  • C (absent puberty at >2.5 SD) is the definition itself.
  • D is also accepted, because the definition covers incomplete puberty as well as absent puberty. Arrested puberty counts.
hippo-endo-Q55:
From 11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function. The two terms describe consecutive stages, each ending at a different cell:

  • Spermatogenesis runs from spermatogonia to spermatids. Spermatogonia renew themselves and make primary spermatocytes by mitosis, then the meiotic divisions end with early spermatids.
  • Spermiogenesis is the maturation of spermatids into spermatozoa, with no further division. Late spermatids shed their cytoplasm as residual bodies, grow a flagellum, and form the acrosome.

Both happen between Sertoli cells, moving from the basal side of the tubule to the lumen.

  • A fails because the two processes are distinct stages.
  • B fails because spermatogonia are the starting cells of spermatogenesis, not its product.
  • C stops spermatogenesis too early and misnames spermiogenesis's product: spermatids are its input, not its output.
hippo-endo-Q56:
From 07 - Development of the Female Reproductive System and 09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation. The development lecture states it directly: female external genitalia are driven by estrogens and the absence of DHT (weeks 9-14). The genital tubercle becomes the clitoris, the urethral folds the labia minora, and the labioscrotal swellings the labia majora, and all three stay unfused. The DSD lecture's split explains why DHT rather than testosterone is the one that matters:

  • DHT builds the external genitalia.
  • Testosterone builds the internal (Wolffian) ducts.

That is why 5α-reductase deficiency gives ambiguous external genitalia with male internal ducts.

  • E (and C) name the wrong androgen. Testosterone's absence governs Wolffian regression, not external genital form.
  • A or B alone is incomplete, because the notes name both factors together.
hippo-endo-Q58:
From 08 - Introduction to Transgender Medicine and 09 - Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis. Gender-affirming hormones have two goals: suppress the endogenous hormone and replace as for a hypogonadal patient. The regimens are asymmetric:

  • Trans women need an anti-androgen (spironolactone, cyproterone acetate) or a GnRH agonist alongside estrogen.
  • Trans men are listed with exogenous testosterone alone, because testosterone suppresses the ovary itself. At therapeutic levels (target 14-24 nmol/L) it exerts negative feedback on the HPG axis, ↓ LH/FSH, and so ↓ ovarian estradiol.
  • A, B fail because a separate estrogen block is unnecessary: the suppression comes free with the testosterone.
  • D reaches the right "no" for the wrong reason. Testosterone does not overpower circulating estrogen at the receptor; it removes the estrogen upstream by shutting down gonadotropins.

hippo-endo-Q59.html:
From 08 - Introduction to Transgender Medicine. The lecture's list of feminizing-therapy (estrogen) risks includes thromboembolic disease (A), gallstones (B) and hypertriglyceridemia (D), as well as ↑ breast cancer and prolactinoma/hyperprolactinemia. These follow from estrogen's hepatic effects: ↑ clotting factors, lithogenic bile, ↑ VLDL. Weight gain (C) and raised liver enzymes (E) are not on the vault's feminizing list, but they sit on the WPATH "likely increased risk" table for estrogen, which is the source this key follows.

  • F fails: polycythemia (erythrocytosis) is testosterone driving erythropoiesis, and the vault lists it under masculinizing risks.
  • G fails: sleep apnea is likewise an androgen effect.

flags.title: Only partly supported by the vault notes
flags.html: 08 - Introduction to Transgender Medicine lists ↑ transaminases under masculinizing risks, not feminizing ones, and does not list weight gain at all. C and E rest on WPATH, not on the vault's notes. This does not contradict the key, but verify it against the slides.

module-endo-Q1:
From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes. D. Insulin deficiency leaves the body behaving as if starving, mobilising stores through glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and lipolysis. The result is weight loss despite an unchanged or increased appetite, one of the three classic early symptoms nearly every new T1DM patient has. Weight gain points away from new T1DM.

  • A (polyuria, including nocturia and new bed-wetting) and C (excessive thirst) are the other two classic early symptoms.
  • B is the unchanged or increased appetite that accompanies the weight loss.
  • E is a late feature: severe hyperglycemia with ketogenesis produces metabolic acidosis (hyperventilation, vomiting), i.e. DKA at presentation, which is common in children.
module-endo-Q2:
From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes. B. She is symptomatic, so one random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L already establishes diabetes. The only question is DKA, which needs the other two legs of the definition: acidosis (blood gas) and ketosis (urine or serum ketones). That is exactly the lecture's workup: random glucose, urine dipstick for glucose and ketones, and a blood gas if DKA is suspected.

  • A and D ask for a fasting glucose, which a vomiting, dehydrated child cannot wait for and which adds nothing in a symptomatic patient. D also omits the blood gas.
  • C and E add A1c or an OGTT. The lecture says FPG and A1c are usually unnecessary in new-onset T1DM, an OGTT in a vomiting child is inappropriate, and neither identifies ketoacidosis.
module-endo-Q3:
From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes. C. With symptoms of hyperglycemia, a single abnormal glucose is enough. Peter has thirst and nocturnal enuresis (polyuria) and a random glucose of 14.7, above the ≥ 11.1 mmol/L random threshold.

  • A: 9.7 is below 11.1, and without symptoms two abnormal values would be needed anyway.
  • B: the glucose is high, but the picture is fever and acute illness, where hyperglycemia and acidosis can be stress-driven, and the stem gives none of the classic osmotic symptoms. (The vault does not discuss stress hyperglycemia; this point is reasoned from general principles.)
  • D: a 2-h 75 g OGTT value of 8.4 is below the diagnostic ≥ 11.1 (it is in the dysglycemia range).
  • E: acanthosis nigricans and obesity mark insulin resistance. They are a reason to screen, not a diagnostic criterion.
module-endo-Q4:
From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes. E. The lecture's target for a patient under 18 with T1DM is A1c < 7.5%, with FPG 4-8 and post-prandial 5-10 mmol/L. The DCCT is why the target exists: lower A1c means fewer long-term microvascular complications. Loki's 8.4% is above it.

  • A and B quote ranges that are not the lecture's targets (4-8 pre-meal, 5-10 post-prandial). The vault gives no separate bedtime target, so A's exact numbers cannot be checked against the notes.
  • C: daily hypoglycemia is never acceptable. Frequent lows mean the regimen needs adjusting.
  • D: A1c reflects about 3 months of glycemia and is checked roughly every 3 months, not annually (frequency reasoned from general principles).
module-endo-Q5:
From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes. B. Loki is on twice-daily NPH plus rapid-acting insulin with an A1c of 8.4%. The DCCT showed that more intensive insulin therapy (basal-bolus or 4-injection schedules) lowers A1c and microvascular complications, and insulin pumps add better control, more reliable absorption, precise dosing and a lower hypoglycemia risk. Intensifying is the lever.

  • A: bolus insulin is dosed before meals on a sliding scale for the planned carbohydrate. Injecting afterwards lets the post-prandial spike run ahead of the insulin (timing reasoned from general principles).
  • C: the dietary pillar is carbohydrate counting matched to bolus dosing, not grazing.
  • D: absorption differs between sites, but restricting to one site does not fix an under-intensive regimen and invites lipohypertrophy (general principles).
  • E: his A1c is above the < 7.5% pediatric target, so something must change.
module-endo-Q6:
From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes. Fix the insulin given before the abnormal reading. Read the table by column, not by day.

  • AC breakfast is high every day (14.7-18.9). The insulin covering the night is the bedtime basal, Levemir, so B: increase Levemir. A (decrease it) goes the wrong way.
  • AC supper is low (3.6, 3.2). The insulin covering the afternoon is the lunch Humalog, so F: decrease lunch Humalog.
  • C: breakfast Humalog governs the AC lunch reading, which is acceptable to low-normal (4.2-8.3). The high breakfast value is a basal problem, not a breakfast-bolus problem.
  • D and E: supper Humalog governs the bedtime reading (5.9-9.3), which needs no change either way.
module-endo-Q7:
From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes and 10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes. A. The lecture's one named screening routine is an annual urinalysis for albuminuria, the earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy.

  • B: screening from diagnosis is the T2DM rule, because T2DM has been present unnoticed for years. T1DM has a datable onset, so screening starts some years after diagnosis (the same 5-year lag applies to nephropathy in 06 - Diabetic Nephropathy).
  • C: blood pressure is checked at every clinic visit (target ≤ 130/80), not once a year.
  • D is backwards. T1DM is autoimmune and clusters with other autoimmune disease, so autoimmune hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's) is more common (association reasoned from general principles).
  • E: lipids matter in T1DM too. The statin rule (≥ 30 years with DM for more than 15 years, or ≥ 40) applies to diabetes of either type.
module-endo-Q8:
From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes and 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes. A is the false statement. The leading cause of death in children with diabetes is DKA, through cerebral edema, which is more common in children, not hypoglycemia. (The ranking itself is general knowledge; the vault states the pediatric cerebral-edema risk.)

  • B is true: treat with about 15 g of fast-acting sugar (tablets, juice, glucose gel via buccal mucosa), with glucagon or IV dextrose if severe.
  • C is true: a low means the insulin covering that interval was too much, so the dose before the low is reduced.
  • D is true: these are the early adrenergic symptoms, the stage at which to treat promptly.
  • E is true: the T1DM sick-day rule is to continue some insulin even when not eating, monitoring glucose and ketones every 2-3 h. Omitting it precipitates DKA.
module-endo-Q9:
From 02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes and 11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes. E is the false statement. Growth hormone is a counter-regulatory hormone that increases insulin resistance, the same reason it raises insulin needs in pregnancy. That is why the lecture's dose table jumps from 0.7-1.0 units/kg/day before puberty to 1.0-2.0 in puberty. Pubertal GH makes control harder by decreasing sensitivity.

  • A, B, C, D are all genuine psychosocial reasons control deteriorates in adolescence: handover of self-management, smoking and alcohol, insulin omission for weight control, and family conflict. (These items are reasoned from general principles; the vault note does not list them.)
module-endo-Q20:
From 04 - Clinically Useful Endocrine Principles and 01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease. True. Exogenous steroid is the commonest cause of Cushing syndrome overall. Glucocorticoids are prescribed for so many inflammatory and autoimmune conditions that iatrogenic cases outnumber every tumour; among endogenous causes, the ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma leads. This is the lecture's fourth question for any functional problem: can this be explained by an exogenous source of hormone? Ask it before ordering a dexamethasone suppression test, because exogenous steroid suppresses ACTH and confounds the workup.

  • B (false) confuses the most common endogenous cause with the most common cause overall.
module-endo-Q21:
From 04 - Clinically Useful Endocrine Principles and 03 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis. True, and the word is thyrotoxicosis, not hyperthyroidism. Thyrotoxicosis is any excess of circulating thyroid hormone, whatever its source. Levothyroxine is widely prescribed and over-replacement is common, so exogenous hormone tops the list. The lecture puts iatrogenic (oral T4) among the thyrotoxic causes and asks of every functional problem whether an exogenous source explains it.

  • B (false) rests on Graves disease, which the thyroid lecture calls "most common". That ranking is among causes where the gland itself makes hormone. Exogenous hormone shows low radioactive iodine uptake, alongside thyroiditis, a separate branch.

The vault never states outright that iatrogenic is commoner than Graves, so the "most common overall" claim rests on this module's own flip card.
module-endo-Q24:
From 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes. A, B, C and D are the lecture's emergency sequence: ABCs and vital signs (A); fluids, starting with normal saline and often many litres because the deficit is very large (C); insulin, always required in DKA; and monitoring every 1-2 h of level of consciousness, Na+, K+, pH and glucose (D). Fluids plus an insulin infusion plus repeated blood draws are why two IV lines are placed (B; the line count is practical rather than stated in the notes).

  • E fails: metformin is an oral T2DM agent with no role in an emergency defined by insulin deficiency. The sick-day rules tell patients to stop it during GI upset, and it carries a lactic acidosis risk in a volume-depleted, acidotic patient.
module-endo-Q25:
From 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes. B. Potassium falls with treatment, not before it. Low insulin drives K+ out of cells, so the initial serum potassium can look normal or high while total-body K+ is depleted. Once fluid and insulin are given, insulin shifts K+ back into cells and serum K+ drops sharply, causing arrhythmias and death. Monitor K+ every 1-2 h and be ready to replace it.

  • A and D: magnesium and phosphate also shift with insulin, but their falls are rarely dangerous and are not what the lecture tells you to watch (general principles).
  • C: sodium is monitored and may look low from hyperglycemic dilution, but it is not the rapidly lethal flux.
module-endo-Q26:
From 06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes. A. Every finding is a small-vessel complication.

  • Tingling and numbness in the feet: peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy (glove and stocking, feet before hands because of nerve length).
  • The slow-healing foot ulcer: a consequence of that neuropathy (loss of protective sensation).
  • "Leaky blood vessels": non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, the most common microvascular complication.
  • B and C need a macrovascular finding (MI or angina, stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease), and the stem deliberately denies chest pain, dyspnea, claudication and stroke/TIA symptoms.
  • D: he clearly has complications.
module-endo-Q32:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs. C. Hypoglycemia risk follows whether the drug releases insulin independently of glucose. Glyburide is a sulfonylurea: it closes the beta-cell ATP-sensitive K+ channel, causing glucose-independent insulin release with a long duration. Hence the rule not to prescribe SUs to the elderly, people living alone or those who drive for a living, and the higher risk in liver or kidney failure.

  • A (metformin) and B (pioglitazone) are insulin sensitizers. They do not change insulin release, so the risk is low or absent as monotherapy.
  • D (repaglinide) acts on the same channel, so it does carry risk, but its rapid onset, short duration and inactive metabolites give a lower hypoglycemia risk than SUs, which is why it suits the elderly better.
module-endo-Q46:
From 11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes. B. Hyperglycemia present during organogenesis (weeks 3-16), i.e. pre-existing diabetes, raises malformations to 2-10%, scaling with A1c at conception. The lecture's cardiovascular list is transposition of the great vessels, coarctation of the aorta, truncus arteriosus, atrial septal defect, pulmonary stenosis and dextrocardia. Tetralogy of Fallot is the one not on it.

  • A, C, D each appear by name in that cardiovascular list.
  • Recall by system: neural tube (spina bifida, anencephaly, caudal regression), cardiovascular, GI (duodenal atresia, imperforate anus), GU (double ureters, renal agenesis).
module-endo-Q47:
From 11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes. C. The pre-conception target is A1c ≤ 7%, ideally ≤ 6.5%, before conception. Tight control before conception cuts anomalies by about 70%, because organogenesis (weeks 3-16) is often under way before the pregnancy is known. Pair it with folic acid and retinopathy screening.

  • A (< 8.0) and B (< 7.5) are too loose. B is the pediatric T1DM target, a deliberate lure.
  • D (< 5.0) sits in the lower half of the non-diabetic range (4-6%): unattainable on insulin without dangerous hypoglycemia, and insulin needs already fall in trimester 1.
module-endo-Q48:
From 11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes. B. Insulin needs fall in trimester 1, with a real risk of hypoglycemia, and the lecture stresses this is not explained by nausea and vomiting. The rule is: the bigger the placenta, the higher the insulin need, and early on the placenta is small.

  • A describes later pregnancy: needs rise slowly in trimester 2 and a great deal in trimester 3, as placental prolactin, cortisol and growth hormone drive insulin resistance.
  • C: requirements change throughout, and drop remarkably after delivery when the placenta is gone.
module-endo-Q49:
From 11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes. B (false). GDM appears at 24-28 weeks, after organogenesis (weeks 3-16) is complete, so it does not raise congenital malformations. That risk belongs to pre-existing diabetes and scales with A1c at conception.

  • A (true) is the lure because GDM infants do share the other morbidities: macrosomia, prematurity, cesarean delivery, neonatal hypoglycemia (the fetus made extra insulin in utero) and hyperbilirubinemia. Morbidity is not malformation.
  • The exception: a "GDM" that does not resolve postpartum was undiagnosed pre-existing T2DM, and that pregnancy did carry malformation risk.
module-endo-Q50:
From 11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes. B (false). The stem is a double negative: mothers with GDM are at increased risk. GDM is unmasked insulin resistance, the pancreas failing to keep up with placental hormones, so it marks a woman with limited beta-cell reserve. Up to 60% of GDM patients develop T2DM long-term, which is why every one is re-screened with a 75 g OGTT at 6 weeks to 6 months postpartum. The same physiology recurs in the next pregnancy, so recurrence is likely too (the recurrence risk is not quantified in the vault; reasoned from general principles).

  • A (true) would make GDM a purely transient event. "Transient, resolves after delivery" describes the hyperglycemia, not the future risk.
module-endo-Q51:
From 11 - Pregnancy and Diabetes. D. The Canadian two-step screen at 24-28 weeks starts with a non-fasting 1-h 50 g challenge: < 7.8 normal, ≥ 11.1 diagnoses GDM, and 7.8-11.0 goes on to a fasting 75 g OGTT. Her 8.8 is in the middle band. On the 75 g test, any one value at or above fasting 5.3, 1 h 10.6 or 2 h 9.0 makes the diagnosis.

  • A: 8.8 is below the ≥ 11.1 that would diagnose on the 50 g test alone.
  • B: 8.8 is above the < 7.8 normal cut-off, so she cannot be cleared.
  • C: A1c is not used in GDM; the lecture says not to check it.
module-endo-Q67:
From 02 - Drugs Affecting Calcium Homeostasis. B and C. Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody against RANKL. Its listed adverse effects are GI upset, back, limb and MSK pain (C), hypocalcemia, ONJ, atypical femoral fracture, and increased infection: cough, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection (B). Immunosuppression is a contraindication for the same reason.

  • A is backwards: every antiresorptive drives calcium down, so denosumab causes hypocalcemia. Hypercalcemia is the signature of the anabolic PTH drug, teriparatide.
  • D: hyperglycemia is not among denosumab's effects.
module-endo-Q68:
From 02 - Drugs Affecting Calcium Homeostasis. A, B and C. rhPTH (teriparatide, the 1-34 fragment) reproduces native PTH's actions: more calcitriol production via renal 1α-hydroxylase (A), better osteoblast survival, the basis of its anabolic effect when given as intermittent daily spikes (B), and more renal calcium reabsorption (C). Together these explain its hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria.

  • D fails: phosphate is the discriminator between PTH and vitamin D at the kidney. Vitamin D retains phosphate; PTH, and so teriparatide, is phosphaturic.
module-endo-Q189:
From 05 - Pathology of Thyroid Masses. A, B, C and F. The question asks what is common, not what matters most. The lecture sorts the thyroid-mass differential into three columns: common (hyperplasia/sporadic multinodular goitre, cyst, Hashimoto's thyroiditis with real nodules and pseudonodules, and adenoma); life- or QoL-threatening (differentiated, poorly differentiated and medullary carcinoma); and urgent (anaplastic carcinoma and lymphoma). Most nodules are benign.

  • D (carcinoma) belongs on the differential, but in the life-threatening column.
  • E (lymphoma) is rare and sits in the urgent column.

module-endo-Q190.html:
From 05 - Pathology of Thyroid Masses. A, B and C. TI-RADS scores what a nodule looks like: composition (A), echogenicity, shape, specifically taller-than-wide (B), margin (C), and echogenic foci. The points give the TR level. In the lecture pathway, a normal or high TSH leads to ultrasound with TI-RADS, and the TR level decides between no follow-up, FNAB or monitoring, and FNAB.

  • D fails: size is not a TI-RADS feature. It enters afterwards, as the threshold for acting on a given TR level (biopsy or follow), so a small suspicious nodule can outrank a large bland one.

flags.html: 05 - Pathology of Thyroid Masses places TI-RADS in the workup but does not list its scoring features. The feature list here comes from the ACR system itself (general principles), not from the lecture note.

module-endo-Q202:
From 07 - Overview of Metabolic Bone Disease. B. Three stem features converge on osteomalacia. Celiac disease is the lecture's named common cause, since fat-soluble vitamin D is malabsorbed; proximal myopathy causing falls is the feature osteoporosis never has; and pseudofractures (healed microfractures) are its radiological hallmark. Expected labs: low calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH, low 25-OH-D and low urine calcium.

  • A: atypical femoral fractures need long-term bisphosphonates, which a 23-year-old is not on.
  • C: a single osteoporotic femoral neck fracture explains neither the weakness nor the falls. Osteomalacia is routinely mistaken for osteoporosis, and the tell is that osteomalacia has overt symptoms while osteoporosis is indolent.
module-endo-Q203:
From 07 - Overview of Metabolic Bone Disease. C. Paget's is disordered remodelling - osteoclastic resorption first, then chaotic new bone - so the treatment is antiresorptive, and the lecture is explicit that IV zoledronate beats oral bisphosphonates. He also meets the treat-even-if-asymptomatic criteria: active disease (↑ ALP) in a long bone. ALP is then the marker you follow on treatment.

  • A - teriparatide is the trap: bone-forming agents are contraindicated in Paget's, because you do not stimulate a formation process that is already abnormal.
  • B - alendronate is the right class by the weaker route; oral bisphosphonates are second to IV zoledronate.
  • D - denosumab has not been studied in Paget's.
module-endo-Q204:
From 07 - Overview of Metabolic Bone Disease. D. osteogenesis imperfecta is a type I collagen defect, and the lecture names IV bisphosphonates (zoledronate) as the mainstay. She also crosses the treatment threshold of more than 3 fractures a year (she has 5). The stem clears the alternatives: normal vitamin D takes osteomalacia off the table, and regular menses mean she is estrogen-replete.

  • A - teriparatide is the anabolic PTH analogue for osteoporosis, not the lecture's OI therapy, and its osteosarcoma signal (in rats) makes it a poor choice in a 17-year-old whose growth plates may still be open.
  • B - denosumab is not the lecture's OI treatment, and its effect reverses when it stops, which suits lifelong fracture prevention in a teenager poorly.
  • C - raloxifene is a SERM for postmenopausal osteoporosis; she menstruates normally, so there is no estrogen deficit to address.
module-endo-Q141:
From 05 - Disorders of Growth. A (True). The lecture's three phases: infancy is fastest (~24 cm in year 1, ~10 cm in year 2, 7-8 cm/yr to age 4), the childhood phase is slowest but longest at ~5-6 cm/yr and is GH-driven, and puberty brings the spurt (~8-12 cm/yr in girls, ~10-14 cm/yr in boys, from sex steroids plus larger GH pulses). Every clause of the statement matches.

  • B would need one of those figures to be wrong, and none is. The clinical use: between age 4 and puberty, a velocity below 4.5 cm/yr is the trigger to investigate, precisely because normal is 5-6.
module-endo-Q142:
From 05 - Disorders of Growth. A (True). Height-age is the age at which this child's height would sit on the 50th percentile, so a taller child has an older height-age and a shorter child a younger one. The lecture's example: a 9-year-old girl at 127 cm has a height-age of 8.

  • B would reverse the direction, and it does not reverse. Keep height-age apart from bone age (a left-wrist x-ray of skeletal maturity): height-age describes size, bone age describes the growth left. In constitutional delay the bone age is delayed and tracks the height-age.
module-endo-Q143:
From 05 - Disorders of Growth. C. Mid-parental height is (mother + father ± 13 cm) / 2, with +13 for boys and −13 for girls. For this girl: (160 + 180 − 13) / 2 = 327 / 2 = 163.5 cm, the 50th percentile. Her genetic target is average, which makes her 1st-percentile height a real departure from it.

  • A (176.5) is the boy's formula: (160 + 180 + 13) / 2.
  • B (160.5) matches no version of the formula.
  • D (170) is the plain parental average with the sex correction left out.
module-endo-Q144:
From 05 - Disorders of Growth. B. The lecture's first question - did the weight fall before the height? - settles it. Weight is at the 75th percentile while height has slid from the 10th to the 1st: a short, relatively chubby child, which is the endocrine pattern. She grew about 1 cm over the interval, far under the 4.5 cm/yr trigger, and she is crossing percentiles after 18 months. Normal birth size plus neonatal hypoglycaemia is the lecture's signature of congenital growth hormone deficiency.

  • A - familial short stature has a normal velocity and a low parental target; her target is 163.5 cm, the 50th percentile.
  • C - illness and undernutrition drop weight first; her weight is preserved, and CBC, ferritin and renal function are normal.
  • D - a height under the 3rd percentile is short stature by definition.
module-endo-Q145:
From 05 - Disorders of Growth. C. This is the endocrine screen for a short, chubby, slowly growing girl. Thyroid function is "the test that must not be missed in any short child", since hypothyroidism slows growth while adding weight. IGF-1 screens for growth hormone deficiency, which her normal birth size and neonatal hypoglycaemia already suggest; confirming it takes two provocative tests, because a random GH is worthless. A karyotype is done in every short girl, for Turner syndrome.

  • A - celiac serology and a GI consult follow the undernutrition pathway, and her preserved weight and normal CBC and ferritin argue against it.
  • B, E - she is under the 3rd percentile and falling off her curve against an average parental target, so neither FSS nor watching fits.
  • D - LH/FSH and sex steroids belong to a puberty workup, not a 7-year-old with no pubertal findings.
module-endo-Q146:
From 05 - Disorders of Growth. B. The lecture's list of genetic causes of short stature is Down syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, Noonan syndrome, Silver-Russel syndrome, Turner syndrome, SHOX mutations, achondroplasia and osteogenesis imperfecta. B is the only option whose three all appear on it. Each distractor is spoiled by one tall-stature syndrome (the lecture does not discuss these; the tall-stature facts are general knowledge):

  • A - Marfan syndrome causes tall stature.
  • C - Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes tall stature with long limbs; Down and SHOX are correct.
  • D - Sotos syndrome is an overgrowth syndrome; Russell-Silver and Turner are correct.
module-endo-Q147:
From 01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease. C. Spells of headache, palpitations and sweating, with pallor, in a hypertensive patient is pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumour, so the screen measures catecholamines and their metabolites. Metanephrines are the better target because secretion is episodic: the parent catecholamine can be normal between spells while the metabolite is not. The lecture's single best screen is plasma free metanephrines (99% sensitive), with urinary metanephrines close behind at 97%; C is the only option that tests the medulla at all.

  • A - the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test screens for Cushing syndrome (cortisol).
  • B - the aldosterone/renin ratio screens for Conn syndrome: resistant hypertension with low K⁺, and no spells.
  • D - haemoglobin tests nothing adrenal.
module-endo-Q149:
From 01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease. Lowest to highest: weight gain (1) → purple striae (2) → hypertension (3) → proximal muscle weakness (4). The lecture ranks Cushing signs by likelihood ratio: general obesity / weight gain 1.75-3.10, purple striae >1 cm 2.72-2.91, hypertension 4.35-5.29, proximal muscle weakness 8-12.6. The key follows that table exactly.

  • The ranking is counter-intuitive on purpose: weight gain is the weakest discriminator, because obesity, hypertension and diabetes are common without Cushing. What separates true Cushing syndrome is ecchymoses, fragility fracture and proximal weakness.
  • Read "likelihood" here as discriminating value (LR), not frequency. Weight gain is the commonest finding, and that is exactly why it discriminates least.
module-endo-Q158:
From 07 - Development of the Female Reproductive System. B. A septate uterus has a normal, fused external contour with a septum dividing the cavity inside it. The ducts fused normally, so the failed step comes after fusion: resorption of the midline septum. It matters clinically because septate is the anomaly most amenable to hysteroscopic resection, and MRI (the external contour) is what separates it from bicornuate.

  • A - independent ducts give uterine didelphys: two uteri and two cervices.
  • C - one absent duct gives a unicornuate uterus: one horn and one tube.
  • D - incomplete fusion gives a bicornuate uterus: a cleft fundus, two horns and one cervix.
module-endo-Q159:
From 07 - Development of the Female Reproductive System. D. uterine didelphys is two separate uteri with two cervices (and a double or single vagina). The paramesonephric ducts never fused and developed separately, which is the most complete fusion failure in the series; the lecture charts it as failed fusion of the inferior ducts, which is why even the cervix is doubled.

  • A - failed septum resorption leaves one uterus with a normal outline and an internal septum (septate uterus).
  • B - partial fusion leaves a shared lower body, one cervix and two horns (bicornuate uterus).
  • C - a single duct gives one horn and one tube (unicornuate uterus).

Didelphys and bicornuate are usually managed expectantly (fertile, with more premature delivery), and the renal tract is imaged with any Müllerian anomaly.
module-endo-Q160:
From 07 - Development of the Female Reproductive System. D. A unicornuate uterus is one horn with one tube; the other side is absent because one paramesonephric duct never developed. On HSG the contrast fills a single narrow cavity that drains to one tube. It carries increased obstetric risk, and since both systems arise from intermediate mesoderm, the renal tract is imaged (the kidney on the missing side is often absent too).

  • A - incomplete fusion is bicornuate: two horns, not one.
  • B - failed septum resorption is septate: a normal outline with a divided cavity.
  • C - independent ducts are didelphys: two complete uteri.

module-endo-Q162.html:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. On a midsagittal female pelvis the lecture names two peritoneal spaces, and Q162 and Q163 almost certainly ask for one each:

  • vesicouterine pouch - anterior, between the uterus and the bladder, where peritoneum reflects from the uterus onto the bladder's superior surface. It is shallow, because the anteverted uterus rests on the bladder.
  • rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) - posterior, between the uterus and the rectum, and the lowest point of the female pelvic cavity when upright. Free fluid, blood or pus collects here, and it is reached by culdocentesis through the posterior fornix, the deepest fornix.

Answer by position: in front of the uterus is vesicouterine, behind it is rectouterine.

module-endo-Q165:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. The letters cannot be checked against the image here, so the value is in locating each structure, front to back on a midsagittal view:

  • Bladder - most anterior, behind the pubic symphysis; the anteverted, anteflexed uterus rests on it.
  • Vesicouterine pouch - the shallow peritoneal recess between bladder and uterus.
  • Uterus - tilted forward over the bladder, its cervix projecting down into the vagina.
  • Vagina - the tube running down and back from the cervix, between the bladder/urethra in front and the rectum behind.
  • Rectouterine pouch - behind the uterus and posterior fornix; the lowest point of the pelvic cavity when upright, so free fluid pools here.
  • Rectum - most posterior, lying in the sacral curve.
module-endo-Q166:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. The letters cannot be checked against the image here. From 01 - Anatomy of the Pelvis and the lecture, the pelvic floor is two muscles and its openings:

  • Levator ani - the large sheet (puborectalis medially, pubococcygeus intermediately, iliococcygeus posterolaterally) that closes most of the floor.
  • Coccygeus - the smaller, posterior part, from the ischial spine to the sacrum and coccyx.
  • Urogenital hiatus - the anterior gap in levator ani. In the female it transmits two structures: the urethra, most anterior behind the pubis, and the vagina just behind it.
  • Rectum - the most posterior opening, through the rectal hiatus, slung by puborectalis.

Order from front to back: urethra, vagina, rectum. That order locates the labels even when the muscles are hard to separate.
module-endo-Q168:
