From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. B. Lymph follows the lecture's nodal watershed: the cervix and uterine body drain to the internal and external iliac nodes, so the iliac basin on the lateral pelvic wall is the first to investigate in cervical cancer.

  • A - Deep inguinal nodes drain the clitoris and vestibular bulb (erectile tissue).
  • C - sacral nodes drain the inferior vagina.
  • D - lumbar (para-aortic) nodes drain the ovary, tubes and fundus, which is why the lecture calls the uterus "one organ, two basins". For the cervix they are a later site, not the first.
module-endo-Q169:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. D. The fundus lies above the pelvic pain line (the lower limit of the peritoneum). Visceral afferents above that line travel back along the sympathetics to the T11/12-L2 dorsal root ganglia. That is why contraction pain is felt in the back, flank and mid-trunk, and why it takes a lumbar epidural (L3/4) to block it.

  • A - the parasympathetic route to S2-S4 serves structures below the line (cervix, upper vagina). It carries cervical dilation pain, not fundal contraction pain.
  • B, C - these mismatch the outflows: parasympathetics leave at S2-S4, never T12-L2, and sympathetics leave at T11/12-L2, never S2-S4.
  • E - the pudendal nerve is somatic, supplying the perineum and lower vagina, so a pudendal nerve block never reaches the fundus. A caudal epidural block (S2-S4) also spares the fundus, and that is why the mother still feels her contractions.
module-endo-Q170:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. A, C and D. A line between the ischial tuberosities, running through the perineal body, splits the perineum in two. The urogenital triangle (pubic symphysis to ischial tuberosities) contains the external genitalia and perineal muscles, is perforated by the urethra (and vagina), and is closed by the perineal membrane (A, C, D). See 01 - Anatomy of the Pelvis.

  • B - the anus perforates the anal triangle (ischial tuberosities to coccyx).
  • E - ischioanal fat fills the ischioanal fossae on either side of the anal canal, which is also the anal triangle.
module-endo-Q171:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. B. A straddle injury drives the perineum up against the pubic arch below the perineal membrane, and the urethra there is the spongy (bulbous) urethra inside the bulb of the corpus spongiosum. That segment runs through the superficial perineal pouch, which is where the lecture puts the leak (Q172).

  • A - the membranous urethra runs through the pelvic floor and deep pouch, inside the external urethral sphincter. It is torn by a pelvic fracture (Q173), not by a straddle.
  • C - the prostatic urethra sits above the pelvic floor, inside the prostate, out of reach of a perineal blow.
module-endo-Q172:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. D. A spongy urethral tear leaks into the superficial perineal pouch, the space between Colles' fascia and the perineal membrane. The attachments decide the spread. Colles is fixed laterally to the fascia lata, so the fluid cannot reach the thigh. It stops at the UG triangle, so the fluid cannot reach the anal triangle. That leaves the scrotum, the penis and the anterior abdominal wall, deep to Scarpa's fascia but superficial to external oblique.

  • A - the anal triangle is sealed off by Colles' fascia's posterior attachment.
  • B - the deep perineal pouch lies above the intact perineal membrane; it fills when the membranous urethra is torn (Q174).
  • C - nothing in the perineum opens into the peritoneal cavity.
module-endo-Q173:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. A. The FAST scan puts fluid in the pelvic cavity, above the pelvic floor, so the tear is in the segment that opens into it: the membranous urethra. It is the narrowest segment, and it crosses the pelvic diaphragm and the deep perineal pouch (urogenital diaphragm) inside the external urethral sphincter. The high-energy crash implies a pelvic fracture, and the membranous urethra is where the fixed urogenital diaphragm shears against the mobile structures above it.

  • B - a spongy tear fills the superficial pouch and abdominal wall, not the pelvis (Q171-172).
  • C - the prostatic urethra is enclosed and protected within the prostate. The shear point in a pelvic fracture is just below it, at the membranous segment.
module-endo-Q174:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. B. A membranous tear leaks into the deep perineal pouch, between the perineal membrane (floor) and the inferior fascia of the pelvic diaphragm (roof). That is the compartment the membranous urethra and external urethral sphincter occupy.

  • A - the anal triangle is posterior and continuous with neither pouch.
  • C - the thighs are closed off by Colles' fascia's attachment to the fascia lata, and that is a limit of the superficial pouch in any case.
  • D - the superficial perineal pouch lies below the intact perineal membrane. It fills with a spongy (straddle) tear, as in Q172.
module-endo-Q175:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. A. The deep pouch's roof is the pelvic diaphragm, and its gap is the urogenital hiatus, the opening in levator ani that transmits the urethra. Fluid in the deep pouch can escape superiorly through that hiatus into the pelvic cavity, which is how a perineal-level tear shows up on a FAST scan.

  • B - the deep perineal pouch is part of the perineum, below the pelvic diaphragm. The pelvic cavity lies above it.
  • C - the anal triangle is posterior, and fluid moving into it would still be below the pelvic floor, not in the pelvis.
module-endo-Q176:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Pelvis. The letters cannot be checked against the image here, so the value is in what identifies each structure:

  • Corpora cavernosa - the paired dorsal columns, holding 80-90% of the blood in erection; proximally they diverge as the crura.
  • Corpus spongiosum - the single ventral column. It expands proximally as the bulb, fixed to the perineal membrane, and distally as the glans.
  • Bulbourethral glands - small paired glands in the deep perineal pouch, beside the membranous urethra.
  • Spongy urethra - the channel running inside the corpus spongiosum, from bulb to glans.

The discriminator: the urethra always travels in the spongiosum, never the cavernosa. A cross-section with one channel in the lone ventral column tells you which is which.
module-endo-Q178:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. A. The pectinate line is the hindgut/proctodeum boundary, and it splits the canal's nerve supply as cleanly as its blood supply. Above it the mucosa is hindgut endoderm with autonomic motor supply and visceral sensory fibres that sense stretch, NOT pain - so an internal hemorrhoid bleeds painlessly. Below it the skin is proctodeal ectoderm supplied by the somatic inferior rectal nerve (from the pudendal nerve), which is extremely pain-sensitive - the territory of the painful external hemorrhoid.

  • B - below the line is the external hemorrhoid, and it hurts.
  • C - right location, wrong nerve type; somatic fibres would make it painful.
  • D - wrong on both counts; the below-line zone is somatic, not autonomic.
module-endo-Q179:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. A. Erection is parasympathetic: S2-S4 fibres leave in the pelvic splanchnic nerves, pass through the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus and become the cavernous nerves, which dilate the helicine arteries; the engorged erectile tissue then compresses its own venous outflow against the penile fascia. "Point and shoot" - Parasympathetic points, Sympathetic shoots. Withdrawal of parasympathetic input is what causes detumescence.

  • B - the pudendal-supplied ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus maintain an erection by compressing venous outflow; they do not produce it.
  • C - somatic sensory input can trigger the reflex (Q180), but the effector is parasympathetic.
  • D - sympathetic output drives ejaculation (Q181), not erection.
module-endo-Q180:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. C. The lecture names two routes to arousal and tells them apart by their trigger. Psychogenic arousal starts in the brain (auditory, visual, olfactory or imaginative stimuli). Reflexogenic arousal is a response to tactile stimulation: its afferent limb is somatic sensory fibres from the genitals (the pudendal nerve, whose dorsal nerve of the clitoris/penis is the primary sensory nerve) entering the sacral cord.

  • A - parasympathetic is the efferent limb shared by both mechanisms, so it does not define the reflexogenic one; it is the answer to Q179.
  • B - somatic motor supplies the perineal muscles, not the arousal trigger.
  • D - sympathetic output is ejaculation (Q181).

Read the key as naming the division that makes the pathway reflexogenic; the arc itself still ends in parasympathetic outflow via the pelvic splanchnics.
module-endo-Q181:
From 06 - Anatomy of the Female Pelvis, Perineum, & Sexual Function. D. Ejaculation is sympathetically mediated - a coordinated contraction of the reproductive tract at orgasm, carried by T11/12-L2 sympathetic fibres through the lumbar splanchnics to the inferior hypogastric plexus. "Point and Shoot" - Sympathetic shoots.

  • A - parasympathetic produces erection (Q179), and its loss causes detumescence.
  • B - somatic motor (pudendal) bulbospongiosus only expels the last drops of semen; the event itself is sympathetic.
  • C - somatic sensory is the reflexogenic trigger (Q180).
module-endo-Q182:
From 09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation. D. A 46,XY infant with an under-virilised 2 cm phallus, fused labio-scrotal folds and a single urogenital opening has testes that made testosterone but external genitalia that never saw enough DHT - the lecture's starred cause, 5-α reductase deficiency. DHT builds the external genitalia and testosterone the internal ducts, so it is ambiguous outside, male inside, and the testes may lie abdominally or inguinally, which fits the impalpable gonads.

  • A, E - in a 46,XY infant CAH adds androgen: boys look normal (penile enlargement, scrotal pigmentation) and present in salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks, not with ambiguity.
  • B - complete androgen insensitivity gives female external genitalia, not a phallus.
  • C - Leydig cell hypoplasia is on the 46,XY list, but with no testosterone the internal ducts fail too; the notes list it without a phenotype, so this split is reasoned from the testosterone/DHT division of labour.
  • F - an androgen-secreting tumour virilises a 46,XX fetus; it cannot under-virilise an XY one.

Confirm with a raised T:DHT ratio after hCG stimulation.
module-endo-Q183:
From 09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation. A, C, D. The lecture's counselling for ambiguous genitalia: gender-neutral terms (gonads, phallus, labio-scrotal folds) until a diagnosis is established (A), and delay sex of rearing, naming and birth registration until investigations are complete, warning that the final diagnosis may take several weeks (D). C is fair for this child: the rest of the exam is normal, and an androgen-action defect in a 46,XY infant is confined to genital differentiation.

  • B fails - sex assignment does not inevitably mean surgery; evidence for the operations is lacking and only expert surgeons should be involved. 5-α reductase deficiency virilises at puberty (60% raised female identify as male), which is exactly why nothing irreversible should be rushed.

C would be the wrong reassurance in salt-wasting CAH, where the adrenal crisis at 1-3 weeks is the danger. Refer to a tertiary multidisciplinary team.
module-endo-Q184:
From 09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation. 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH. The key only fits if the case moved to the 46,XX side of the tree (a virilised XX infant) or showed a markedly raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone. CAH from 21-hydroxylase deficiency is 95% of all CAH and the commonest cause of a virilised 46,XX infant: cortisol blocked → ACTH ↑ → adrenal hyperplasia → precursors shunted to androgen → clitoral hypertrophy, labial fusion, at worst a single urogenital opening. The same enzyme sits on the aldosterone limb, so 75% salt-waste (Na↓, K↑, acidosis, hypoglycaemia), with crisis at 1-3 weeks.

  • Discriminators: 17-OHP markedly raised (the case ran 400 against < 10); ovaries and female internal genitalia on ultrasound; hyperpigmentation from ACTH excess.
  • Management: lifelong hydrocortisone 10-15 mg/m²/day plus fludrocortisone, oral saline in infants, and stress dosing in illness.
module-endo-Q185:
From 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS). A, B, D. Each keyed sign traces to a PMOS mechanism. Visceral (central) adiposity (A) is the metabolic phenotype, and peripheral fat converts adrenal androgen to testosterone. Cystic acne (B) is hyperandrogenism. Dark skin over the back of the neck (D) is acanthosis nigricans, the lecture's insulin-resistance sign, often with skin tags beside it.

  • C fails - as the module says, fine hair on the lower arms and upper lip can be normal. The hirsutism that counts is terminal, male-pattern hair on the face, chin, anterior chest and upper arms, judged against rate of onset, ethnicity and parental appearance.
module-endo-Q186:
From 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS). B, C. Read each result as either an exclusion or a limb of the triad. Prolactin 10 is under the lecture's normal ceiling of < 20, so hyperprolactinaemia is excluded (B). Testosterone 2.5 is fractionally over the female normal of < 2 nmol/L - the mildly raised level that fits PMOS (C).

  • A - a raised beta-hCG means pregnancy, the first mimic to exclude; the plan forks on it.
  • D - 10 nmol/L is inside the male range (from ~8), which points to an androgen-secreting tumour, especially with rapid onset; it needs DHEAS and imaging.

A normal testosterone would not exclude PMOS either - clinical hyperandrogenism satisfies the limb on its own.
module-endo-Q187:
From 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS). A, B, C, E. The lecture lists exactly these as more common in PMOS: endometrial carcinoma (A), from unopposed estrogen with infrequent bleeds - hence withdrawal bleeds at least 4× a year; central adipose distribution (B), the insulin-resistance phenotype; gestational diabetes (C), part of the same metabolic risk as T2DM; and frontal alopecia (E), an androgen effect.

  • D fails - adrenal hypertrophy is not a PMOS feature; it is the distractor. Adrenal hyperplasia belongs to CAH, a PMOS mimic separated by a raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
module-endo-Q188:
From 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS). A, B, C, D. PMOS is treated by the symptom of distress. Oral contraceptives (A) regulate the cycle, protect the endometrium and appear under three of the four complaints; androgen blockers - spironolactone, cyproterone (B) - treat hirsutism and alopecia; surgical reduction in ovarian stromal mass - partial resection, drilling, thermal ablation (C) - is for subfertility, marked "rare now" but still keyed; aromatase inhibitors (D) induce ovulation.

  • E fails - topical testosterone (Androgel) adds androgen to a syndrome of androgen excess, worsening hirsutism, acne and alopecia. It is the only wrong answer.
module-endo-Q194:
From 08 - Introduction to Transgender Medicine. B. The lecture's persistence split is the point: most PRE-pubertal children who identify as transgender do not persist into adulthood; most ADOLESCENTS do. That is why the treatment ladder starts at puberty (Tanner 2), and pre-pubertal children get social support, not hormones.

  • A - prevalence is rising, not falling (1.2-4.1% of adolescents; 1 in 300 Canadians aged 15+).
  • C - reverses the split: once puberty has started, identity usually persists.
module-endo-Q195:
From 08 - Introduction to Transgender Medicine. B, C. The ladder runs in order of reversibility. Puberty blockers (GnRH agonists such as leuprolide) are the fully reversible first stage once puberty has started: they pause the physiological hormone effect while persistence declares itself (B). Fertility preservation is discussed BEFORE hormones start (C), not after.

  • A - testosterone effects are NOT fully reversible; voice and hair changes persist, so hormones are only partially reversible.
  • D - co-existing mental health conditions must be "reasonably well-controlled", not resolved.
  • E - genital surgery waits for the age of majority, but top surgery can be done at 16 after a year of hormones, so "not before 18" is too absolute.
module-endo-Q196:
From 04 - Disorders of Puberty and 06 - Adolescent Development. D. A breast that has grown beyond the areola but still forms one smooth contour with it is Tanner III; in Tanner IV the areola and papilla lift into a secondary mound, and Tanner II is only a bud. The 12 cm/yr velocity agrees: girls hit their growth spurt between Tanner 2 and 3.

  • A - Tanner I has no glandular tissue, and a prepubertal child does not grow 12 cm/yr.
  • B - Tanner V is the adult breast, with the areola back in the breast contour and a projecting papilla.
  • C - Tanner II is a breast bud with surrounding glandular tissue only; a full mound is further along.

Mid-puberty at 7 is precocious (girls < 8) - the thread Q199-200 pick up.
module-endo-Q197:
From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. B (False). Two errors in one statement. CDGP is the commonest cause of delayed puberty in boys, but its bone age is DELAYED - and that delay is what makes the diagnosis; an advanced bone age points away from it. And CDGP boys enter puberty late, at 14-18; initiation at 10-14 is simply normal timing (boys 9-14).

The rest of the CDGP picture: height at or below the 3rd percentile with a normal growth velocity, a strong family history, low-normal LH/FSH, and a normal adult height - so the treatment is reassurance.
module-endo-Q198: From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. A (True). Gonadotropins split every hypogonadism: high LH/FSH with low sex steroid means the gonad has failed and the pituitary is shouting (primary hypogonadism); low LH/FSH means the brain never sent the signal (secondary). Turner syndrome (45,X in 60%) is the typical girl: streak ovaries, short stature, pubarche in 100% (adrenal) but menarche in only 1%, and most need estrogen to enter puberty at all. Karyotype is diagnostic; the boys' counterpart is Klinefelter syndrome.
module-endo-Q199:
From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. B. Every value says the axis itself has switched on. Random LH 5.1 is far above the > 0.3 mIU/L that signals central puberty; FSH has risen with it; estradiol 120 against < 40 is pubertal; and a bone age of 10 in a 7-year-old is advanced. Raised gonadotropins with raised sex steroid, and signs in the normal order, define central precocious puberty.

  • A - GnRH-independent (peripheral) precocity has suppressed LH and FSH with high sex steroid; here the gonadotropins are high.
  • C - breast development before 8 is precocious in a girl, and these levels are abnormal for 7.

The GnRH stimulation test (peak LH > 5) is the gold standard if the random LH were equivocal.
module-endo-Q200:
From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. C. In girls, central precocious puberty is mostly idiopathic (idiopathic/sporadic/familial - rare in boys), and Q199 has already made this central: LH and FSH are raised.

  • A - a hypothalamic hamartoma is a CNS-dependent cause of CPP, but those are more common in boys; with no neurological features it is not the likeliest in a girl.
  • B, D, E - environmental estrogen, an ovarian cyst and McCune Albright syndrome are all peripheral causes: sex steroid rises independently of GnRH, so LH and FSH would be suppressed, not 5-6.

Treat with an LHRH analogue; untreated idiopathic CPP costs an average 5-6 cm of adult height.
module-endo-Q201:
From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. B. This is central precocious puberty in a boy: onset before 9, testes 8-10 mL (bilaterally ≥ 4 mL means LH is driving the Leydig cells), and LH, FSH and testosterone all far above Tanner 1 ranges. In boys fewer than 50% of CPP cases are idiopathic - hypothalamic or pineal tumour, hamartoma, hydrocephalus, trauma and radiation must be sought - so MRI head is mandatory.

  • A - puberty at 7 is precocious by definition in a boy.
  • C - calling it idiopathic without imaging is the error; the idiopathic default belongs to girls. The LHRH analogue comes after the MRI.
  • D - peripheral testosterone would suppress LH/FSH and leave the testes small (< 3 mL); both are the opposite here.
module-endo-Q205:
From 03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty. C. Before puberty the axis is built but held down: GABA inhibition dominates glutamate, and LH secretion is fairly constant across the 24 hours. Puberty is disinhibition - kisspeptin/GPR54 signalling rises, pulsatility restarts, and the earliest measurable change is a nocturnal LH rise.

  • A - the gonads are responsive; the LH/FSH surge of fetal life and the first months after birth drives them.
  • B - the pituitary can make gonadotropins, as that same neonatal surge shows; it is unstimulated, not incapable.
  • D - boys do not grow faster; peak height velocity is the same in both sexes, and boys end taller because they start later.
  • E fails because C is correct.
module-endo-Q206:
From 11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function and 03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty. A. Breast development splits cleanly between the two ovarian steroids: estrogen builds the DUCT systems; progesterone builds the lobules and alveoli.

  • B - backwards: estrogen increases the uterine muscle's responsiveness, and it is progesterone that quiets the myometrium. The notes do not state this; reasoned from general principles.
  • C - after ovariectomy LH and FSH are high from lost estradiol feedback (as after menopause); giving estrogen restores the feedback and lowers them.
  • D - estradiol drives endometrial proliferation; it increases growth rather than decreasing it.
  • E fails because B-D are false.
module-endo-Q207:
From 03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty. E. Same principle as Q205: before 8 the limiting step is the hypothalamus. GnRH output is suppressed and LH secretion is fairly constant; puberty needs pulsatile GnRH, which returns when kisspeptin/GPR54 signalling lifts the GABA brake, showing first as a nocturnal LH rise.

  • A - target tissues respond to sex steroids at any age; peripheral precocious puberty proves it.
  • B - the gonads respond to gonadotropins, as the neonatal LH/FSH surge shows.
  • C - the pituitary makes gonadotropins in the fetus and first ~6 months of life; it is unstimulated, not incapable.
  • D - nothing blocks the gonads; the restraint is on GnRH itself (GABA dominance, with MKRN3 inhibitory).
module-endo-Q208:
From 11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function and 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS). B. Bioactive androgen is the free fraction (only ~5% of testosterone is unbound), so it rises with more production or less binding. More adrenal androgen (B) raises it - the adrenal is one of the lecture's hyperandrogenism sources, through non-classic CAH, an adrenal tumour, or peripheral fat converting adrenal androgen to testosterone.

  • A - granulosa cells do not make androgen; they aromatise the theca cells' androgen into estrogen. The LH-driven theca cell is the ovarian androgen source.
  • C - more SHBG binds more testosterone and lowers the bioactive fraction - the opposite of her picture. Estrogen raises SHBG, which is part of why the OCP helps hirsutism.
  • D, E fail because only B is right.
module-endo-Q209: From 02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease. Bitemporal hemianopia. The optic chiasm sits directly above the sella, and the fibres crossing in it are the nasal retinal fibres, which carry each eye's temporal field. A macroadenoma growing up out of the sella presses the chiasm from below and cuts those crossing fibres, so both temporal fields go. This is the mass-effect half of every pituitary question (the other half is hormone excess or deficiency): document it with formal visual fields, and ask too about diplopia (CN III/IV/VI), headache and apoplexy.
module-endo-Q210:
From 02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease. D (prolactin 800). A prolactin of 800 µg/L is far above the macroadenoma threshold of ~200, so this is a prolactinoma - and the prolactinoma is the one pituitary macroadenoma treated medically first: a dopamine agonist (cabergoline, bromocriptine) shrinks it and the field defect lifts. A visual field defect is not an indication for surgery here.

  • A (urine cortisol 800) - Cushing disease → transsphenoidal surgery.
  • B (TSH 6 with free T4 32) - a non-suppressed TSH beside a high free T4 suggests a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, also surgical; the notes do not cover it, so this is reasoned from general principles.
  • C (testosterone 3) - hypogonadism from compression of the normal gland; it needs replacing but does not argue against operating.
  • E (IGF-1 800) - acromegaly → transsphenoidal surgery first.
module-endo-Q211:
From 02 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease. B. Acromegaly does not make you taller. It is GH excess after the epiphyses have closed, so IGF-1 drives acral and soft-tissue growth - enlarging hands and feet, coarse features, frontal bossing, gapped teeth, macroglossia - not height. GH excess before plate fusion would be gigantism.

  • A - heart failure occurs in 3-10%, from cardiomyopathy; cardiovascular complications drive the excess mortality (SMR 1.72 untreated).
  • C - obstructive sleep apnea is on the lecture's complication list, which is why a sleep study is part of the workup.
  • D - enlarging hands (rings no longer fit) is the classic acral change.
module-repro-Q50:
From Approach to Common Breast Problems. The breast exam always includes the axilla, because most of the breast's lymph drains there and the axillary tail of Spence is breast tissue. In Pathology of the Breast, axillary node status is the most important prognostic factor once distant metastases are excluded - so for a 55-year-old post-menopausal woman with a new lump (investigate now), the axilla is the priority region.

  • A fails: parasternal (internal mammary) nodes drain the medial breast but are not palpable in practice.
  • C, D are examined in the same sweep (infra- and supraclavicular), but they are second-echelon nodes, not the primary basin.
  • E fails: cervical nodes are not a breast drainage basin.
module-repro-Q51:
From Approach to Common Breast Problems. She is pre-menopausal, not high risk, and the history and exam are benign - a small, mobile, tender, cystic mass found late in the cycle (LMP 3 weeks ago, i.e. luteal phase, when cyclical tissue is most swollen and tender). The lecture's rule: re-examine after the next menstrual cycle, and investigate only if it has not resolved.

  • B fails at this point: ultrasound is the right first image for a woman < 35, but only once the lump persists after the cycle.
  • A, D fail: tissue sampling (core or FNA) skips the benign-pathway step entirely for a lesion likely to be cyclical change or a cyst.
module-repro-Q52:
From Approach to Common Breast Problems. The workup skeleton is history + breast exam + axilla and nodes, with imaging chosen by age: at 39 (> 35) it is mammogram first ± ultrasound. Being adopted means her family history is unknown, so she cannot be reassured as low risk and the lump is investigated rather than watched. A neck, chest and abdominal exam looks for nodal and distant spread (lung, pleura, liver, bone).

  • C fails: CA-125 is an ovarian marker, not a breast test.
  • D, G fail: CT is staging, not initial assessment; MRI is reserved for high-risk women < 35 or BRCA carriers.
  • E fails: Her2/neu is a special test on tissue from a confirmed carcinoma (see Pathology of the Breast).
  • I, L fail: she has no discharge and no signs of infection.
  • J, K, N fail: pelvic exam, β-hCG and urinalysis answer no question raised by a painless breast lump.
module-repro-Q58: From Second Trimester Ultrasound. The module gives three reasons to look for anomalies, and all three are the options: counsel the parents on what to expect, direct further investigations (genetic testing or detailed imaging antenatally, or postnatal workup), and decide the place of delivery and level of care the finding needs. Birth defects affect 2-3% of all pregnancies and many are now diagnosed antenatally; the scan is a screen, so a finding leads to more testing rather than a diagnosis - which is why B is a purpose in its own right.
module-repro-Q72:
From Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding. Endometrial carcinoma must be excluded in every woman with PMB, and a Pap only screens the cervix - it does not sample the endometrium. The workup proceeds regardless: speculum exam, TVUS (normal < 5 mm), and endometrial biopsy for > 5 mm, any PMB, or recurrent bleeding. The lecture states it directly: a negative Pap does NOT end the workup.

  • B fails because stopping at a negative Pap would miss the most serious causes - hyperplasia and carcinoma - which present with bleeding in 90% of endometrial cancers.
module-repro-Q73:
From Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding. Insufficient endometrial tissue is not a benign result. Endocervical fragments mean the sampler reached the canal, not the cavity, so the endometrium - where carcinoma must be excluded in every woman with PMB - has not been assessed at all. The lecture's pathway sends an insufficient sample straight to repeat sampling, by you or a gynecologist (hysteroscopy or D&C).

  • A fails because "benign" needs tissue to be benign; calling a non-sample reassuring is exactly the error the module is testing.
  • C fails because a failed office biopsy is an indication to re-sample by another route, not for hysterectomy - there is no diagnosis yet to operate on.
module-repro-Q74:
From Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding. Atrophy is the most common cause of PMB, and scant atrophic endometrium is a benign report - but atrophy is a pathologic diagnosis of exclusion that must fit the TVUS and the exam. So she is reassured, offered treatment for the atrophy (local estrogen - cream, pill or ring - or nothing if not troublesome), and told to come back if bleeding persists or recurs, because recurrent bleeding re-opens the workup.

  • B fails: unlike report #1, this sample did reach the endometrium and gave a diagnosis; "scant" is what a thin atrophic lining yields, not an inadequate sample.
  • C fails: nothing on the report raises the cancer risk; hysterectomy is for atypia or carcinoma.
module-repro-Q75:
From Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding. The atypia line decides it: without atypia the management is medical, with atypia it is surgical. Atypical hyperplasia carries an 8-29% malignancy risk, and 30-40% of patients have a concurrent adenocarcinoma found at hysterectomy - so she is referred to gynecology for hysterectomy + BSO, with high-dose progestin only if surgery is contraindicated.

  • A fails: hyperplasia is the precursor of type 1 (endometrioid) carcinoma, not a benign endpoint to watch.
  • B fails: the sample was diagnostic. Progestin plus a repeat biopsy at 3 months is the plan for hyperplasia without atypia.
module-repro-Q76:
From Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding. Endometrioid adenocarcinoma is cancer - the commonest type (90%) of endometrial carcinoma, estrogen-dependent, with hyperplasia as its precursor. Treatment is hysterectomy + BSO with staging (± lymphadenectomy, and radiation or chemotherapy by grade and stage), so she is referred to a gynecologist.

  • A fails by confusing two words: endometrial names the site, endometrioid names the histologic type - neither means benign.
  • B fails: a biopsy showing carcinoma already is the tissue diagnosis; repeating it only delays surgery.
module-repro-Q78:
From Pathology of 1st Trimester Bleeding. The lecture's branch point is what the ultrasound shows inside the uterus: a gestational sac in the cavity with no fetal heart is a spontaneous abortion. Bleeding, cramping and a positive β-hCG all fit, and a closed cervix with a retained non-viable sac is the missed pattern. Confirmation is products of conception on pathology.

  • A fails: ectopic is no sac in the uterus plus an adnexal mass; an intrauterine sac is the opposite finding.
  • C fails: a complete mole is a "snow storm" with no fetus, a uterus large for dates and a markedly raised hCG - she has a sac and only a slightly enlarged uterus.
  • D fails: an endometrial polyp is an anatomic (PALE) cause of bleeding and cannot explain a positive hCG.
module-repro-Q84:
From Hysterectomy Approaches. Every approach is planned as a "short stay" with same-day discharge except abdominal, which is the only one that is not minimally invasive and needs a 2-3 day hospital stay. It is reserved for complex cancers, a very large uterus, patient factors that block a minimally invasive route, or complications during a minimally invasive attempt.

  • A fails - vaginal is the most minimally invasive route (no abdominal incision) and is same-day.
  • C fails - robotic enters the abdomen but is minimally invasive and same-day; it replaces abdominal, not vaginal.
  • D fails - LAVH enters the abdomen but delivers the uterus vaginally; same-day.
module-repro-Q101:
From Dilation and Curettage. Asherman's syndrome is adhesions in the endometrial cavity after curettage, presenting as secondary amenorrhea (and, with a scarred cavity, infertility). Risk is 8% after one curettage, rising to 30% by a third consecutive procedure - why sharp and repeat curettage are avoided.

  • B fails - hematometra (post abortal syndrome) is blood accumulating in the cavity right after the procedure; it is re-evacuated immediately, not a late scarring problem.
  • C fails - retained products are tissue left behind, managed with a second D&C or misoprostol; it is a cause of repeat curettage, not the adhesions.
  • D fails - cervical shock is a transient vasovagal reaction to the paracervical block, lasting minutes.
module-repro-Q102:
From Dilation and Curettage. A D&C is vacuum aspiration of a pregnancy under 14 weeks, with two indications: first-trimester pregnancy loss (incomplete, inevitable, missed) and therapeutic abortion under 14 weeks. A missed abortion is a non-viable intrauterine gestation still in the cavity, so evacuating it is exactly what the procedure does.

  • A fails - an ectopic pregnancy has nothing in the uterine cavity to aspirate; the gestation is in the tube.
  • B fails - the procedure is defined as < 14 weeks; later terminations need a different approach.
  • D fails - endometritis is treated with antibiotics; instrumenting an infected uterus is not a treatment (infection is itself a D&C complication).
module-repro-Q104:
From Approach to Preterm Labour.

  • B is true - morbidity and mortality are gestational-age dependent: the earlier the birth, the more RDS, IVH, NEC, sepsis and death.
  • C is true - multifetal gestation (twins) is a listed risk factor, via pathologic uterine distension.
  • D is true - preterm birth drives prolonged NICU stays, which carry a high cost to the healthcare system, so preventing it can save money overall.
  • A is false - previous spontaneous preterm birth is the leading risk factor; a prior event raises the risk in subsequent pregnancies.
module-repro-Q105:
From Approach to Preterm Labour. The lecture states it directly: amniocentesis for bacteria is NOT a validated test for rupture of membranes. Bacteria in the fluid speak to intra-amniotic infection (chorioamnionitis), not to whether the membranes are open - and an invasive needle test is not how rupture is confirmed. Diagnosis is history plus bedside findings.

  • A is validated - low amniotic fluid on ultrasound supports rupture.
  • B is validated - pooling in the posterior fornix on speculum exam.
  • D is validated - a positive nitrazine test: alkaline amniotic fluid turns the paper blue.
  • E is validated - a positive ferning test on a dried slide.
module-repro-Q106: From Approach to Preterm Labour. All five are listed PPROM consequences - there is no distractor. The main risk is preterm birth (B): under 32 weeks without treatment, 50% deliver within 48 h and 75% within 7 days. The open membranes let infection ascend - ↑ chorioamnionitis (A); the sudden drop in intrauterine pressure predisposes to placental abruption (D); and loss of fluid lets the cord slip past the presenting part - umbilical cord prolapse (C), an emergency. Because PPROM brings birth forward, it carries the consequences of prematurity, including a prolonged NICU stay (E).

workbook-repro-Q144.html:
From Infant Nutrition. The vault's growth chart gives the rule: a newborn loses 5-10% of birth weight on days 1-3 (fluid shift, low early colostrum volume) and regains birth weight by 10-14 days. The discriminator is therefore the regain time, not the loss: ~10% is the ceiling of normal loss, but nobody is back to birth weight in 3-5 days - that is when the nadir occurs.

  • A, E (15%) exceed the normal ceiling; a 15% loss is pathological and should prompt feeding/dehydration assessment.
  • B (10%, 3-5 days) confuses the timing of the nadir with the timing of recovery.
  • C (5%, 7-10 days) understates the upper limit of normal loss.
  • D (10%, 7-10 days) is the best available option: correct loss ceiling, regain time nearest the notes' 10-14 days.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: Infant Nutrition states regain of birth weight by 10-14 days, which contradicts the keyed B (3-5 days) and favours D. Key left as printed.

workbook-repro-Q1.html:
From Development of the Female Reproductive System. C wins by elimination: it is the only option that is not an internal duct. Female external genitalia develop in weeks 9-14, driven by estrogen and the absence of DHT, from the swellings around the urogenital sinus's opening: genital tubercle → clitoris, urethral folds → labia minora, labioscrotal swellings → labia majora, all three staying unfused. The sinus itself gives the lower 2/3 of the vagina via the sinovaginal bulbs.

  • A fails: the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts form the tubes, uterus, cervix and upper 1/3 of the vagina - all internal.
  • B, D fail: one structure under two names (mesonephric = Wolffian), which degenerates without testosterone and leaves only remnants such as Gartner's duct.

flags.title: The key is loosely worded
flags.html: Development of the Female Reproductive System derives the external genitalia from the genital tubercle, urethral folds and labioscrotal swellings, not from the urogenital sinus, which gives the lower 2/3 of the vagina. C is still the best of the four (the others are internal ducts), so the key stands - but learn the tubercle / folds / swellings mapping, not "sinus → external genitalia".

workbook-msk-Q59:
From Anatomy of the Back & Spinal Cord. The vault's counts are 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, a sacrum of 5 fused segments and a coccyx of 4 fused. C is the only option with both numbers right. The spinal-cord lecture gives a cross-check: there are 8 cervical spinal nerves for 7 cervical vertebrae (C8 exits below C7), whereas the 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar nerves match their vertebrae one-to-one.

  • A fails: cervical is 7, not 4.
  • B fails: it hands the cervical count (7) to the thoracic region; lumbar is 5.
  • D fails: the coccyx is 4 fused segments; 5 is the sacrum.
  • E fails: neither is a single bone's worth of segments - sacrum 5, coccyx 4.
workbook-msk-Q64:
From Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus. The claw is the ulnar nerve's signature, from loss of the intrinsic hand muscles, and the lecture puts the ulnar nerve on the medial cord carrying C8 and T1 only - the inferior trunk. That shared root is the link to Klumpke's palsy: a lower plexus injury (C8-T1, classically after shoulder dystocia) takes out the ulnar supply at its origin and produces the same claw.

  • A fails: the radial nerve (posterior cord, C5-T1) gives wrist drop, not a claw.
  • B fails: the median nerve (all five roots) gives thenar weakness, not the ulnar claw.
  • D fails: the upper plexus (Erb's palsy, C5-C6) is the Q61 answer and spares the hand.
workbook-msk-Q84:
From Colles fracture and Smith's fracture. Two discriminators settle every distal-forearm eponym: the mechanism and the direction of the distal fragment. A Colles fracture is the FOOSH (fall onto outstretched hand) injury with dorsal angulation of the distal radius - exactly this stem, in the older patient the workbook's own Q78 describes.

  • A fails: Smith's fracture is the reverse - volar displacement, from a fall on a flexed wrist or a blow to the dorsum.
  • B fails: Monteggia is a proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation - the elbow, not the wrist (Q82).
  • C fails: Barton is an intra-articular rim fracture of the distal radius with carpal subluxation; nothing here says intra-articular.

workbook-msk-Q85.html:
From Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus. Reasoned answer (mine, not the workbook's): A, tentatively. The vault's brachial plexus notes name the two classic patterns - upper (Erb's palsy, C5-C6) and lower (Klumpke's palsy, C8-T1), both after shoulder dystocia - but never say which is commoner. In general the upper-trunk injury is the commoner pattern (traction that widens the neck-shoulder angle), and its territory is the deltoid and biceps: the axillary nerve and the musculocutaneous nerve. Of those, A is the more defensible, and E is nearly as good.

  • B, C each draw on all five roots (Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus), so a partial plexus injury rarely silences either completely.
  • D is the lower-plexus nerve (C8-T1): the less common pattern, even though it is the likely "intended" answer after Q64.

Not a letter to memorise - the question has no single defensible answer as written (see the flag on this question).

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The vault does not cover this question's load-bearing fact; the reasoning is from general principles and should be checked against the lecture or the facilitator.

workbook-msk-Q86:
From Anatomy of the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity. The stem names the nerve, so the thinking worth doing is about the level. The lecture gives the median nerve two compression sites: through pronator teres at the elbow (pronator syndrome) and under the flexor retinaculum at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome). Flexor pollicis longus, the lateral FDP and pronator teres are all supplied above the carpal tunnel, so their weakness places the lesion proximally - even though night-time paresthesia sounds like carpal tunnel.

  • A fails: the radial nerve supplies the extensors (wrist drop), none of the listed flexors.
  • B fails: the ulnar nerve supplies the medial FDP and the intrinsics (claw), not FPL or pronator teres.
  • D fails: the axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor at the shoulder.
workbook-msk-Q20:
From Fracture Management and Fracture Radiology. An open (compound) fracture exposes the bone or fracture hematoma to the external environment through a break in the skin, so it is contaminated by definition. The lecture lists its cost: ↑ infection, non-union, delayed union and incomplete recovery, worst after high-energy trauma. That is why management aims to convert an unstable, contaminated wound into a stable, clean one - early antibiotics and tetanus, debridement and irrigation, early closure. A closed fracture keeps the soft-tissue envelope intact and does better.

  • A gets the outcomes backwards.
  • C, D swap the definitions: it is the open fracture that is contaminated.

Any wound near a fracture, even a distant one, counts as open until proven otherwise.
workbook-msk-Q72:
From Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder. Rotator cuff disease is progressive, and the vault's spectrum ends in rotator cuff arthropathy: a massive cuff defect lets the humeral head migrate superiorly until it touches the acromion, and arthritis follows. That end stage is Stage IV in the workbook's scheme (Q71), and it is the stage treated by shoulder arthroplasty rather than cuff repair.

  • A-C are the earlier steps - inflamed intact tendon, partial tear, full tear - all before the joint itself degenerates.
  • E fails: there is no Stage V; the option is never used in Q71-74.
workbook-msk-Q73:
From Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder. Stage II is the first structural defect: a partial-thickness defect of the supraspinatus tendon at its articular end (not the bursal end) - the "mild tear". It follows from the lecture's intrinsic mechanism: vascularity is lost from the articular portion of the tendon distally, so that is where fibres fail first. Cuff repair is reserved for Stage II-III disease that fails conservative care.

  • A fails: Stage I is an inflamed tendon that is still structurally intact.
  • C fails: Stage III is full thickness.
  • D, E fail: arthropathy is the end stage, and Stage V does not exist.
workbook-msk-Q74:
From Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder. Stage III is a full-thickness supraspinatus defect - the "severe tear". With the cuff no longer holding the head down, the humerus displaces superiorly and synovial fluid can leak into the surrounding tissue (swelling). It is still short of the massive defect and arthritis that define arthropathy.

  • A fails: Stage I is intact but inflamed (the impingement stage, the one acromioplasty treats).
  • B fails: partial thickness is Stage II.
  • D fails: Stage IV is arthropathy - massive defect, head riding up to the acromion, arthritis.
  • E fails: there is no Stage V.
workbook-neuro-Q137:
From Summary Notes - Neuro. The stem's triad - ≥ 15 minutes, more than one seizure in 24 hours, or focal onset - is the vault's definition of a complex febrile seizure, set against the simple febrile seizure (generalized, < 15 minutes, one in 24 hours, drowsiness under 30 minutes, no workup). Complex ones matter because they warrant MRI or CT and carry a higher epilepsy risk.

  • A fails: simple is the opposite on every criterion.
  • C fails: status epilepticus is defined by duration alone (the notes give benzodiazepines from 5 minutes), is not specific to fever, and has no "focal" or "twice in 24 hours" criterion.
  • D fails: "febrile focal seizure" is not a category - focality is one of the three criteria that make a seizure complex.
workbook-neuro-Q138:
From Approach to Stroke and Approach to Localization. Reasoned answer (mine, not the workbook's): C, with the side corrected - a right internal capsule lesion. Hemiparesis of face, arm and leg together with no sensory symptoms is the pure motor stroke, one of the five lacunar syndromes in Approach to Stroke, and Approach to Localization lists "pure motor hemiparesis (face = arm = leg)" as a subcortical sign of a lenticulostriate occlusion. The motor fibres are packed together in the internal capsule, so one small infarct catches all three regions and spares sensation. Left-sided weakness needs a right-sided lesion, and every option says "left", so none is strictly correct.

  • A fails: a cortical lesion spreads face, arm and leg across a wide strip and brings cortical signs with it.
  • B fails: the thalamus gives the pure sensory stroke - the opposite deficit.
  • D fails: the insula is not primary motor cortex (the key's own false premise).

workbook-neuro-Q131.html:
From Neuroradiology. Diagnosing hydrocephalus means showing the enlarged ventricles and their cause (an obstruction to CSF flow or over-production). MRI has the best contrast resolution (+++) of the modalities in the lecture, with fluid dark on T1, bright on T2 and CSF suppressed on FLAIR - so it shows the ventricles, the obstructing lesion and the periventricular edema best, without radiation.

  • A fails as the gold standard: CT is the fast, widely available first look when ICP is up, at the cost of lower contrast resolution and radiation.
  • C fails: a plain x-ray shows bone, not ventricles.
  • D fails: ultrasound sees the ventricles only through an open fontanelle in infants - a screen, not the standard.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The vault does not cover this question's load-bearing fact; the reasoning is from general principles and should be checked against the lecture or the facilitator.

workbook-psych-Q27:
From Cognitive Disorders in the Elderly. The vault ranks them outright: Alzheimer's disease is the most common type of dementia, 60-90% of all dementia; vascular dementia is second; frontotemporal dementia is fourth, about 5%; and DLB is a few percent (though under-diagnosed).

  • B is the serious distractor: mixed pathology is common, but the notes rank Alzheimer type first as the diagnosis.
  • C fails: vascular is second.
  • D, E fail: FTD and DLB are each a small fraction.

hippo-msk-Q11.html:
From 02.2 - Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain. New saddle anesthesia on a background of bilateral leg and back pain is a neurologic red flag, and red flags are the one situation where back pain gets imaged. The picture is cauda equina syndrome (the notes list it among the spine problems to recognize; 03.2 adds MRI when there is significant neurologic compromise), a surgical emergency where decompression is time-critical.

  • A fails: mechanical back pain is a diagnosis made only once red flags are absent.
  • B fails: physiotherapy is conservative care, which red flags override.
  • D fails because C is right.

review.t: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain

hippo-msk-Q4.html:
From 01 - Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus. A blow to the elbow with numbness in the little finger is the ulnar nerve at the "funny bone", behind the medial epicondyle. The ulnar nerve comes off the medial cord, so it carries only C8 and T1 (the inferior trunk).

  • A (C5-T1) is the whole plexus, and the roots of the median and radial nerves, not the ulnar.
  • B (C5-C7) is the lateral-cord pattern (e.g., musculocutaneous), which spares the little finger.
  • D (C7) is a single root whose dermatome is the middle finger, not the fifth.

hippo-msk-Q45:
From 08 - Physical Activity Prescription. The lecture lists the cardiovascular benefits of regular activity: ↑ oxygen uptake, ↑ oxygen utilization, ↑ endothelial function, ↑ plasma volume and ↓ blood viscosity, with ↑ stroke volume, ↓ resting heart rate and ↓ blood pressure on the heart side.

  • A, D are on that list verbatim.
  • B fails on the word during: the ↓ BP is a chronic training effect. Acutely, blood pressure rises with exertion, which is why the notes require BP under 180/100 before starting and warn that strenuous resistance work can push LV pressure over 300 mmHg.
  • C is the reverse of the lecture: viscosity falls.
hippo-msk-Q67:
From 06 - Osteoarthritis. OA treatment is staged first (early, late, end stage), then goes in order: non-pharmacologic, pharmacologic, surgical. Arthroplasty is a salvage procedure for end-stage disease no longer controlled by other therapies, and early OA starts with active, neuromuscular-control exercise (Tai Chi is the lecture's example), weight loss and assistive devices.

  • A fails: early-stage disease is not an indication for replacement.
  • B fails: the notes say only arthroplasty has real benefit; arthroscopy is not recommended.
  • C fails: early OA is actively treated (exercise, weight management, topical NSAIDs), not just watched.

hippo-msk-Q68.html:
From 06 - Osteoarthritis. The OA drug list marks opioids "generally avoid": tramadol has some evidence but its risks have to be weighed, and opioids sit in the Not recommended box. 03 - Rheumatology Treatments adds why: opioids do nothing for inflammation and bring cognitive impairment, constipation and dependence.

  • A fails: topical and oral NSAIDs are first-line approved OA treatments (topical is inconclusive only for the hip).
  • C fails: an intra-articular steroid injection is listed for short-term relief.
  • D fails: duloxetine is the SNRI to try when other therapies fail.
  • B (oral prednisone) is not on the OA list at all, but it is not what the lecture flags to avoid.

flags.title: B is not an OA treatment either
flags.html: 06 - Osteoarthritis lists only intra-articular steroids; systemic prednisone is a rheumatology drug for inflammatory disease (03 - Rheumatology Treatments). The key's E is the option the notes explicitly say to avoid, but do not read B as endorsed for OA.

hippo-msk-Q70.html:
From 07 - Approach to Polyarthritis. The distribution table is the discriminator: MCP joints point to RA, and the DIP joints are usually SPARED in RA and other connective tissue diseases. Symmetric small- and large-joint involvement completes the RA pattern.

  • A fails: OA is one of the diseases that does hit the DIPs (with the 1st CMC).
  • B fails: seronegative disease is axial (SI joints, spine) with asymmetric large joints, and psoriatic arthritis also targets the DIPs.
  • C fails: infection is typically a single hot joint, not a symmetric small-joint pattern.

hippo-msk-Q2.html:
From the spinal disc herniation note linked from 02.2 - Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain. A paracentral lumbar herniation (the most common kind) compresses the nerve of the lower vertebra, so L5/S1 hits S1. Only a far lateral herniation catches the upper root.

  • A fails: L4 would need an L3/L4 paracentral or an L4/L5 far-lateral herniation.
  • B fails: L5 is the upper root at this level, hit only if the disc were far lateral.
  • D fails: S2 is a level below the traversing root.

Posterior-thigh pain fits an S1 radiculopathy; 03.2 would confirm it with a lateral-foot sensory change, weak plantar flexion and a reduced Achilles reflex.

review.t: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain

hippo-msk-Q8.html:
From 05.2 - Clinical Approach to the Elbow. The embedded elbow dislocation note says posterior dislocation is most common, so the statement that anterior is more common is the false one.

  • B is true: the typical mechanism is a FOOSH (or bracing in a car crash).
  • C is true: of the nerves, the ulnar nerve is the one the note singles out, as it runs right behind the medial epicondyle.
  • D is true: compartment syndrome is listed with capsule rupture, ligament tears and broken skin, which is why the note calls it an emergency.

hippo-msk-Q32.html: Break the position down joint by joint. The elbows are bent, so elbow flexion. The humerus swings behind the trunk, which is shoulder extension. The forearms turn inward so the hands meet at the small of the back, which is internal (medial) rotation. Bringing the two wrists together behind the body draws the arms toward the midline, which is adduction, not abduction. The vault's muscle notes put this exact combination in one muscle: latissimus dorsi (from 02.1 - Anatomy of the Back & Neck) "extends, aDDucts and medially rotates the humerus". That is the hand-behind-the-back movement, and why the lats and teres major are what the cuffs load.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key lists shoulder aBduction. Reaching behind the back to bring the hands together is adduction with extension and internal rotation, the actions the vault's latissimus dorsi and teres major notes give. Extension, internal rotation and elbow flexion in the key are right; read the abduction as an error.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture works through this position; the reasoning is from the muscle actions in the anatomy notes and general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

hippo-msk-Q53.html:
From 09 - Connective Tissue Disorders. Each complication is a signature of one disease:

  • A → iii (myositis): pharyngeal and cardiac muscle involvement (aspiration, arrhythmia) plus the paraneoplastic link of dermatomyositis in the elderly.
  • B → iv (Sjogren's): ↑ risk of non-Hodgkin, specifically MALT lymphoma.
  • C → i (SLE): 50x cardiovascular risk; accelerated atherosclerosis is the commonest cause of death, worsened by steroids.
  • D → ii (scleroderma): significant ILD in ~15%, tracked by anti-Scl-70.
  • E → ii (scleroderma): renal crisis in diffuse disease (RNA-polymerase), now rarer thanks to ACE inhibitors.

flags.title: The key looks wrong on D
flags.html: The key maps interstitial lung disease to SLE and scleroderma. 09 - Connective Tissue Disorders and its embedded disease notes attach ILD to scleroderma, myositis (anti-Jo1) and Sjogren's; the SLE lung section lists pleuritis and pulmonary capillaritis, not ILD. Scleroderma is the safe answer for D; SLE is not supported by the notes.

flags.title: A matching question scored as one letter
flags.html: This is a matching exercise, but the bank scores it as if A alone were the answer. The key line gives the full mapping; check yourself against every pair, not just the letter.

hippo-msk-Q55.html:
From 09 - Child with a Limp and 04 - Pediatric Orthopedics. Age plus one hallmark sorts each:

  • A → i (transient synovitis): ages 3-10, a viral URTI 7-10 days earlier, sudden unilateral hip pain, the hip held flexed, abducted and externally rotated, afebrile.
  • B → iii (Osgood-Schlatter): traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity in active 8-14 (F) / 10-15 (M) year olds; x-ray shows the "teardrop" sign.
  • C → iv (SCFE): adolescent, gradual hip pain referred to the knee, left more often than right, painful weight-bearing.
  • D → ii (Legg-Calve-Perthes): ages 4-8, low birth weight, gradual vague hip pain, stiffness and limb-length discrepancy from femoral-head osteonecrosis.

The stem's protein S/C deficiency is not in the vault note; its risk factors are family history, low birth weight and second-hand smoke.

flags.title: A matching question scored as one letter
flags.html: This is a matching exercise, but the bank scores it as if A alone were the answer. The key line gives the full mapping; check yourself against every pair, not just the letter.

hippo-msk-Q65.html:
From 04 - Acute Monoarthritis and the MSK summary notes. An acute pseudogout (CPPD) attack is treated like an acute gout attack: NSAIDs (indomethacin), colchicine, or steroids (intra-articular or oral prednisone). What does not carry over from gout is urate lowering (allopurinol), which is for gout only.

  • A (colchicine) is on the vault's acute-attack list for pseudogout.
  • B, D are both listed: IA injection and a short oral prednisone taper.
  • C is an NSAID; a COXIB belongs to the same class as the indomethacin in the notes.

So on the vault notes, every option is an appropriate treatment for CPPD.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key says colchicine is inappropriate because it is a gout drug. The MSK summary notes list colchicine for acute pseudogout attacks, and the Schulich MSK review notes it on the slide (SR slide 115), although the embedded pseudogout note leaves it out. Colchicine is used in CPPD, so no option here is clearly inappropriate. The key's distinction is allopurinol, not colchicine.

hippo-msk-Q69.html:
From 07 - Approach to Polyarthritis. The lecture's rule is flat: whenever the sacroiliac joint is involved, think seronegative spondyloarthropathy (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic, IBD-associated, reactive). Axial disease with asymmetric large peripheral joints is their pattern, and inflammatory back pain (better with movement, worse in the second half of the night) goes with it.

  • A, B fail: CTD arthritis and RA are symmetric small- and large-joint peripheral diseases.
  • D fails: OA targets weight-bearing joints, the 1st CMC and DIPs; its spine disease is facet OA, not sacroiliitis.

hippo-neuro-Q16:
From 05 - Cranial Nerve Anatomy and Function. CN VIII carries two sensory functions, hearing and balance, and the note tests each: a hearing test, the Romberg sign, and assessment for nystagmus.

  • A, B are the hearing tests: 04 - Hearing Loss pairs Weber (lateralizes) with Rinne (separates conductive from sensorineural) and says to always do both.
  • C tests the vestibular half: an acute vestibular loss produces nystagmus.
  • D is listed for CN VIII too: with the eyes closed, balance rests on vestibular input plus proprioception, so a vestibular lesion can unmask a positive Romberg.
hippo-neuro-Q19:
From 06 - Facial Anatomy. The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of V3 that runs with the superficial temporal artery and vein, supplying the skin in front of the ear, the temporal scalp and the TMJ.

  • A (frontal, V1) gives off the supraorbital nerve to the forehead.
  • B (infraorbital, V2) supplies the midface through the infraorbital foramen.
  • C (mental, V3) supplies the chin through the mental foramen.
  • D (great auricular, C2-C3) supplies the angle of the mandible and is the one facial territory outside the trigeminal nerve.
hippo-neuro-Q20:
From 06 - Facial Anatomy. The great auricular nerve comes from the cervical plexus (ventral rami of C2 and C3) and supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the one patch of the face the trigeminal nerve does not cover.

  • A (frontal, V1) is the forehead.
  • B (infraorbital, V2) is the midface and upper lip.
  • C (mental, V3) is the chin and lower lip, anterior to the angle.
  • E (auriculotemporal, V3) is in front of the ear and the temporal scalp.
hippo-neuro-Q21:
From 06 - Facial Anatomy. The sphincters are named for the opening they surround: orbicularis oris surrounds the lips and closes the mouth; it is orbicularis oculi that closes the eye. That makes C the incorrect pairing.

  • A is correct: frontalis (occipitofrontalis over the frontal bone) raises the eyebrows.
  • B is correct: zygomaticus major pulls the corners of the mouth up into a smile.
  • D is correct as the lecture states it: platysma helps depress the mandible.
  • E is correct: occipitalis moves the scalp.
hippo-neuro-Q22:
From 06 - Facial Anatomy. The muscles of mastication act on the TMJ and are supplied by V3, not the facial nerve. The lecture names masseter (strongly closes and protrudes the jaw) and temporalis (closes and retracts it).

  • B fails: the orbicularis muscles are facial-expression sphincters of the mouth and eye (CN VII).
  • C fails: the zygomatici raise the corners of the mouth.
  • D fails: buccinator helps chewing by keeping food between the teeth but is a muscle of facial expression; platysma is too.
hippo-neuro-Q23:
From 06 - Facial Anatomy. CN VII splits in the parotid into five branches, each matched to the muscle it supplies, and every pairing here matches the lecture:

  • A Temporal → occipitofrontalis (frontalis), plus the upper orbicularis oculi.
  • B Zygomatic → zygomaticus major, plus the lower orbicularis oculi.
  • C Buccal → buccinator, plus part of orbicularis oris.
  • D Marginal mandibular → the inferior orbicularis oris.
  • E Cervical → platysma.

D is the one to hesitate on: orbicularis oris has two supplies (buccal above, marginal mandibular below), so both pairings are correct.
hippo-neuro-Q45:
From 10 - Cortical Syndromes. Broca's area is in the inferior frontal lobe, next to motor cortex, so its aphasia is a motor (expressive) deficit. Wernicke's area is in the posterior temporal lobe, next to auditory cortex, so its aphasia is a sensory (receptive) deficit in understanding. Fluency does not follow comprehension: a Wernicke patient producing nonsense words is still fluent.

  • A swaps the deficits and puts Wernicke's in the parietal lobe.
  • B swaps both the lobes and the deficits.
  • D puts Broca's in the parietal lobe and gives Wernicke's the expressive deficit.
hippo-neuro-Q47:
From 02 - Neurophysiology of Vision. The lecture defines glaucoma as raised intraocular pressure compressing the axons of retinal ganglion cells, the axons that form the optic nerve. It takes peripheral vision first, giving "tunnel vision". (06 - Monocular Vision Impairment refines this: glaucoma is the optic neuropathy itself, and it can occur at normal pressure.)

  • A fails: cataract is clouding of the lens from misfolded proteins.
  • B fails: Horner syndrome is a sympathetic-chain lesion (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), not a pressure problem.
  • C fails: macular degeneration is deposits or new vessels under the fovea, distorting central vision.
  • E fails: myopia is a refractive error.

hippo-neuro-Q48.html:
From 08 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex. Memory is distributed:

  • A The hippocampus forms new memories and converts short-term to long-term; bilateral loss (patient H.M.) causes anterograde amnesia.
  • D The amygdala, anteromedial to it, has an integral role in emotion, learning and memory.
  • B, C The prefrontal cortex is a multimodal association area responsible for working memory, and association cortex links new input to memories of past experience.

All four count.

flags.title: B and C are only partly in the notes
flags.html: 08 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex credits the prefrontal cortex with working memory but never names the medial frontal or ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Keying B and C as correct is reasonable, but it rests on treating them as prefrontal subregions, not on anything the note says about them specifically.

hippo-neuro-Q56:
From 13 - Neuroembryology. A newborn without a skull or the front of the brain is anencephaly: failed closure of the cranial neural tube, so parts of the brain and skull never form. There is no treatment, almost all affected babies die shortly after birth, and folic acid in pregnancy is preventive.

  • B fails: lissencephaly is a migration defect giving a smooth cortex with few gyri; the skull is there.
  • C fails: microlissencephaly is the same smooth brain with a small head at birth, still with a skull.
  • D fails: polymicrogyria is too many small folds, with the cortex reduced from 6 layers to 2-3.
hippo-neuro-Q65:
From 05 - Neuropathic Pain. The lecture opens by separating nociceptive pain (tissue injury, somatic or visceral) from neuropathic pain (a nervous-system lesion or dysfunction), and says the two are not treated the same way. NSAIDs target inflammatory tissue pain and are absent from its neuropathic list.

  • A is listed: amitriptyline, a TCA that also helps sleep and is the cheapest option.
  • C is listed: gabapentin, an anticonvulsant and the classic choice for postherpetic neuralgia.
  • D is listed: capsaicin, topical, applied 3x daily.
  • E is listed under "Other": cannabinoids.
hippo-neuro-Q90:
From 05 - Movement Disorders. The lecture's mnemonic for Parkinson's disease is TRAP: Tremor at rest, starting on one side; Rigidity, which increases with augmentation; Akinesia and bradykinesia (hard to start movement, slow movement); Postural instability (poor balance).

  • A fails: tumor, aphasia and paresthesia are not parkinsonian features.
  • B fails on P: paresis (weakness) is not a feature, since strength is preserved in PD.
  • D fails: tumor and "polyrheumatica" are distractors (polymyalgia rheumatica is a rheumatology diagnosis).
hippo-neuro-Q103:
From 06 - Monocular Vision Impairment. Glare and halos around lights that make night driving worse are the classic symptoms in the embedded cataract note. Cataract is opacity of the lens, the leading cause of reversible blindness, and fully treatable with lens replacement. At 55 it fits the age.

  • B fails: glaucoma is silent until late, then takes peripheral vision first. It does not cause glare.
  • C fails: vitreous hemorrhage (e.g., proliferative diabetic retinopathy) gives sudden floaters or vision loss, with dark mobile spots in the red reflex.
  • D fails because A fits.

The car accident is incidental; it is simply when the driving problem came up.
hippo-neuro-Q107:
From 04 - Hearing Loss. The lecture lists the drugs that damage cochlear hair cells or CN VIII: platinum chemotherapy (cisplatin, carboplatin), aminoglycosides, and loop diuretics (furosemide). Aspirin can cause a temporary, reversible ototoxicity.

  • A, B, C are all on that list individually, so the combined option that holds all three is right.
  • D fails: it leaves out the loop diuretics.

These drugs cause a sensorineural loss, so Weber lateralizes to the better ear.
hippo-neuro-Q108:
From 05 - Vertigo. In BPPV a loose otoconium drifts into a semicircular canal (usually the posterior canal, since it sits lowest). The note's features follow from that:

  • A is true: episodes are brief, under a minute, in the seconds-to-minutes row of the duration table.
  • B is true: attacks are triggered by head movement (looking up, rolling over in bed), and are diagnosed with Dix-Hallpike and cured with Epley.
  • C is false: BPPV is purely vestibular, with no hearing loss and no vision loss.

So D (A and B) is right, and E fails for including vision loss.

hippo-neuro-Q111.html:
From 06 - Approach to Headache. An aura is a transient, reversible neurologic disturbance that comes before or with the migraine. The vault's migraine note gives the classic form as visual: photopsia and transient visual loss (B). A sensory aura, spreading numbness and tingling (C), is the other common type, though that goes beyond the note.

  • A fails: coma is an altered level of consciousness, a red flag for a secondary cause, not an aura.
  • D fails: fever with headache points to infection (e.g., meningitis), not migraine.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key marks all four options, including coma and fever. Neither is a migraine aura: 06 - Approach to Headache and its migraine note describe the aura as visual (photopsia), and fever or reduced consciousness with headache are warning signs of something else. The defensible answer is B and C.

hippo-neuro-Q113:
From 01 - The Dying Patient and MAiD. Among the safeguards the lecture lists, two independent clinicians must certify eligibility (the note says two physicians), after a written request witnessed by an independent party.

  • A fails: patients must be at least 18 and mentally competent.
  • B fails: consent is given at the request and again at the time of MAiD, unless a waiver of final consent was signed (allowed only in the stream where natural death is reasonably foreseeable).
  • D fails: MAiD can happen at home, in long-term care or in hospital. Hospital is typical only when organ donation follows.

hippo-neuro-Q114.html:
From 08 - Pediatric Ophthalmology. A white reflex (leukocoria) means something white sits behind the pupil or in front of it, so anything opacifying the path of light can cause it. The lecture names retinoblastoma (the retinal cause that must not be missed) and congenital cataract (an anterior cause). Retinopathy of prematurity produces it when advanced disease leaves a scarred or detached retina.

  • A, B, C are each a cause, so D is right.

Any abnormal red reflex in a child needs urgent ophthalmology referral. Remember the one benign mimic: an off-axis light (~15°) can reflect off the optic nerve and look white.

flags.title: C is not in the vault notes
flags.html: 08 - Pediatric Ophthalmology names retinoblastoma and congenital cataract as causes of leukocoria but does not mention retinopathy of prematurity. That part is from general principles; verify it before relying on it.

hippo-neuro-Q11.html:
From 08 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex. The sensory homunculus gives cortex to body parts by receptor density, not size, so the densely innervated face (lips, tongue) and hands (fingertips) get the largest areas of the postcentral gyrus. The motor homunculus follows the same logic for fine movement, and the hands dominate there too.

  • A fails: the hands are large but the arms are not.
  • B fails: legs and feet sit on a small strip on the medial surface (ACA territory).
  • D fails: the trunk is tiny; the genitals are represented but small.

hippo-neuro-Q12.html:
From 04 - Introduction to Neuroanatomy. The three planes: a coronal cut runs side to side, like a slice of bread, so both hemispheres, the ventricles and (further back) the hippocampi appear together, symmetric about the midline. An axial cut is parallel to the horizon. A sagittal cut runs front to back and shows one hemisphere in profile.

  • A would show a side-on profile with the corpus callosum as an arch.
  • C, D are the same plane (transverse is another name for axial), which is a hint that neither can be the single answer.

flags.title: The image is missing
flags.html: The source question showed a brain image that is not in the portal, so the key cannot be checked against it. The explanation gives the rules for telling the planes apart; the letter comes from the bank.

hippo-neuro-Q26.html:
From 03 - Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem, Basal Ganglia, and Diencephalon. Each disease targets a different part of the dopamine and basal ganglia circuit.

  • 1, Parkinson's → C, substantia nigra: the midbrain's dopamine-producing neurons are lost, the direct pathway becomes hypoactive, and thalamic output falls (bradykinesia).
  • 2, Huntington's → A, striatum: the caudate and putamen degenerate, the indirect pathway goes quiet, and thalamic output rises (a hyperkinetic disorder).
  • 3, Schizophrenia → B, nucleus accumbens: the accumbens is the ventral striatum, a limbic dopamine target. 07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology ties positive symptoms to excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway.

The trap is that the accumbens is also striatum. Huntington's is a movement disorder of the dorsal striatum (caudate and putamen).

review.t: Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem, Basal Ganglia, and Diencephalon

hippo-neuro-Q29.html:
From 03 - Psychotic Disorders & Schizophrenia (Week 19). Positive symptoms are experiences people normally do not have, added on top of normal mental life. Negative symptoms are a loss of normal function.

  • A, B are positive symptoms. Hallucinations and delusions are the lecture's core examples, alongside disorganized thinking and excitement.
  • C, anhedonia (reduced pleasure) is a loss of function, so it is negative.
  • D, alogia (reduced spontaneous speech) is also negative.

The rest of the negative list is flattened affect, avolition, anergia, asociality, inattention and ambivalence. The split matters because first-generation antipsychotics treat only the positive symptoms.

hippo-neuro-Q37.html:
From 04 - Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum. Two of the three long tracts cross in the medulla. Only the pain pathway crosses as soon as it enters the cord.

  • Corticospinal → medulla: 90% of axons cross at the pyramidal decussation into the lateral corticospinal tract. The other 10% stay ipsilateral in the anterior tract.
  • Medial lemniscus → medulla: the second-order neurons in the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus send their axons across as the medial lemniscus.
  • Spinothalamic → spinal cord entry: the first-order neuron synapses in the dorsal horn at once, and the second-order axon crosses in the anterior white commissure.

This split is why a hemicord (Brown-Séquard) lesion causes ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception but contralateral loss of pain and temperature.

review.t: Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum

hippo-neuro-Q41.html:
From 12 - Approach to Localization. Once a lesion is placed in the brain, the lecture sorts it by signs that only one level can produce. Aphasia heads the list of cortical signs, followed by neglect, apraxia, cortical sensory loss (agraphesthesia, astereognosis) and isolated homonymous hemianopia. Language depends on the cortex of the dominant hemisphere.

  • B, subcortical lesions cause pure motor or pure sensory hemibody deficits (face = arm = leg) or ataxic hemiparesis, and language is spared.
  • C, brainstem lesions cause vertigo or diplopia plus another sign, or crossed face-versus-body sensory loss.

Do not confuse word-finding difficulty (aphasia) with slurred speech (dysarthria). Dysarthria can come from any of the three levels and leaves comprehension, naming, repetition and fluency intact.

hippo-neuro-Q43.html:
From 07 - Anatomy of the Cranial Cavity, and the vault's cavernous sinus note. The contents of the cavernous sinus are the internal carotid artery (with its sympathetic plexus) and CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI. That is why compression, whether by thrombus, pituitary mass or carotid aneurysm, causes ophthalmoplegia, orbital and facial pain, chemosis and trigeminal sensory loss.

  • B (CN IV), E (CN V2), F (ICA): all run through the sinus, so all are affected.
  • A, optic chiasm: not a content of the sinus.
  • C, CN VIII: runs in the internal acoustic meatus of the posterior fossa.
  • D, CN V3: leaves through the foramen ovale and does not pass through the sinus.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key includes A, optic chiasm. Neither 07 - Anatomy of the Cranial Cavity nor the vault's cavernous sinus note places the optic pathway in the sinus. Its contents are the ICA and CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI, so the supported answer is B, E, F. The vault's cavernous sinus note mislabels the ophthalmic nerve as “CN II”, which may be how the chiasm got into the key.

hippo-neuro-Q46.html:
From 02 - Neurophysiology of Vision. Accommodation is the lens changing shape to keep the image focused on the retina. The ciliary muscles change its shape through the suspensory fibres. When they contract, the lens rounds up for near vision. When they relax, the lens flattens for distance.

  • B: the iris and pupil control how much light enters (the pupillary light reflex), not focus.
  • C: only half right. The pupil constricts along with accommodation (both are driven by CN III through the ciliary ganglion) but does no focusing itself.
  • D: light passes through the cornea first, but the lecture gives the focusing change to the lens.
  • E: the fovea receives the image, and the posterior chamber is a fluid space.

hippo-neuro-Q54.html:
From 04 - Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum. Pain, temperature and crude touch travel in the spinothalamic tract. Its first-order neuron synapses in the dorsal horn right away. The second-order axon crosses in the anterior white commissure at the level of entry, then ascends on the opposite side to the thalamus.

  • B: wrong tract. The dorsal columns carry fine touch, vibration and proprioception.
  • C: right tract, wrong crossing point. The medulla is where the dorsal column pathway crosses, as the medial lemniscus.
  • D: accurate for the dorsal columns, but they do not carry pain or temperature.

Learn each tract together with where it crosses, because the crossing point is what localizes a cord lesion.

review.t: Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum

hippo-neuro-Q61.html:
From Schulich Reviews - Neuro (01 - Approach to Head Injuries). Severe head trauma starts with the ABCDE primary survey under C-spine precautions, with intubation if GCS is below 8, followed by a STAT CT. CT is fast enough to find a hematoma that needs surgery. MRI takes too long and is impractical in an unstable trauma patient, so it comes later, once the patient is stable and the CT is done.

  • A: protecting the airway and spine is the first step.
  • B, C: large-bore IV access and bloodwork are part of circulation in any major trauma resuscitation. The review names the survey, not these specifics.
  • D: STAT non-contrast CT head is the first-line imaging.

hippo-neuro-Q62.html:
